4472e6cc41b5507c: LOS ANGELES, Oct — Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-winning actress who starred in classic Hollywood films including “On the Waterfront” and “North by Northwest,” died Tuesday, her publicist said. She was 102 years old.

Over her seven-decade career the ever-elegant Saint caught the eyes of influential filmmakers, including Alfred Hitchcock and Elia Kazan, building a legendary resume in film as well as television, which also earned her an Emmy.
Her representative Jeff Sanderson said Saint died of natural causes at home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family and loved ones.
Saint’s performance in “On the Waterfront” was her film debut, and earned her the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.

Kazan’s crime drama with music composed by Leonard Bernstein is widely considered among the greatest films of all time, featuring an all-star cast including Marlon Brando, who also scored an Oscar for his role.
The 1954 film catapulted Saint, who played the ethereal foil to Brando’s seething macho boxer, to Hollywood fame.
She went on to star opposite Cary Grant in Hitchcock’s masterpiece “North by Northwest.”
Saint was considered a surprise choice to play a Hitchcock blonde, the double agent femme fatale who beguiles Grant.
But she pulled it off, even though she never worked again with the Englishman, who was notorious for putting his leading ladies through hell and for controlling his actors to the last detail.
“He worked with me from the outside in,” she later said.
“My hair, my makeup, my shoes, my jewellery, my purse, my gloves, everything. And just from creating that exterior for me, he gave me the sense of a spy lady.”
Timeless performance
Saint’s storied career also included work with director Otto Preminger, when she played opposite Paul Newman in “Exodus” in 1960.
Two years later she was Warren Beatty’s love interest in John Frankenheimer’s “All Fall Down.”

With Hollywood at her feet, Saint “could have been a contender” for superstardom – to echo the most famous line from “On the Waterfront” – but instead she chose to step back to raise her family with director Jeffrey Hayden.
Indeed her eldest son, Darrell, was born just two days after she won her Oscar.

The brilliance of Saint’s incarnation of Edie, whose brother is lured to his death by the Brando character, has come to be seen by critics as the stand-out performance of a film once revered for its male roles.
The restrained Saint could not have been more different to the intense method mumbling of Brando.
“He was adorable – really adorable, but a little frightening,” she later said of her enigmatic co-star.
“I felt that he could see right through me,” she told Turner Classic Movies (TCM) in 2013.
More than half a century later, Saint made a big screen comeback as Superman’s adoptive mother in the 2006 blockbuster “Superman Returns,” when she was in her early 80s.

And she was still busy into her mid-90s, playing a small part in the supernatural fantasy “Winter’s Tale” alongside Colin Farrell and Russell Crowe, and as a mother superior in the nun drama “Mariette in Ecstasy,” which came out in 2019.

But having first developed her acting chops in live television dramas, TV remained her preferred medium. She won an Emmy in 1990 for her role as a rich widow in the acclaimed miniseries “People Like Us.”
65-year marriage
Saint was born on July 4, 1924 in Newark, New Jersey, to Quaker parents whom she credited with developing her sense of discipline.
She entered Bowling Green State University with plans to become a teacher but left with a degree in dramatic arts after discovering a passion for theatre.
Saint trained in New York at the Herbert Berghof Studio and then the Actors Studio – the home of method acting – which was co-founded by Kazan.
A rarity among Hollywood couples, she and Hayden’s marriage lasted for 65 years until his death in 2016.
With two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, Saint said her longevity had brought extra depth to her work.
“The longer you live, the smarter you get, because you’ve been around, you’ve seen things.
“You’ve gone through different emotional experiences in your own life, and hopefully, you understand things better,” she told TCM.
“And that makes you a better actress.” — AFP
e7d973bbe6529a30: OCTOBER 7 — There is a tendency in contemporary geopolitics to assume that the United States and China must necessarily approach artificial intelligence from opposite directions.
Washington innovates, Beijing competes; one side accelerates and the other responds. Such a framework is becoming increasingly inadequate.

China has demonstrated that it understands one of the central dangers confronting humanity: artificial intelligence that becomes increasingly autonomous, militarised and ultimately difficult for human beings to control.
This matters enormously as the technological competition moves beyond generative and agentic AI towards what may eventually become super intelligence.

At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in late May, Major General Meng Xiangqing of China’s National Defense University issued an important warning. The militarisation of emerging technologies, including AI, he argued, was challenging traditional rules governing warfare and creating the danger that events could escape human control.
This should not be dismissed as diplomatic rhetoric.

A senior figure associated with the People’s Liberation Army was acknowledging something that every major power must eventually confront. The danger posed by advanced AI does not originate merely from who develops the most powerful system first.
It arises when increasingly autonomous systems become embedded in military command, intelligence, cyber operations and potentially nuclear decision-making.
The speed of machines is fundamentally different from the speed of diplomacy.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The United States and China are competing for technological supremacy while confronting shared risks from increasingly autonomous artificial intelligence. — Pixabay pic

Human beings hesitate. Diplomats consult. Military commanders seek clarification. Presidents can pick up telephones. Even during the most dangerous moments of the Cold War, human judgment sometimes prevented technological warnings or incorrect intelligence from escalating into catastrophe.
Super intelligence could compress this decision-making space dramatically.
Imagine autonomous systems detecting what they interpret as preparations for an attack.
Another AI system detects the response. Both begin recommending countermeasures. Cyber systems intervene. Satellites, drones and autonomous weapons respond almost instantaneously.
The danger is no longer simply artificial intelligence. It is machine-speed escalation.
This is why China’s acknowledgement of the problem deserves serious attention.

Beijing does not appear to be arguing that AI development should stop. Nor would such a position be realistic. China, the United States and other technologically sophisticated powers understand that AI will transform productivity, medicine, logistics, manufacturing, scientific discovery and national security.
The distinction must therefore be between controlled technological advancement and uncontrolled technological escalation.

Generative AI is not necessarily the principal systemic danger. Neither is agentic AI by definition. Both can certainly create serious problems, particularly when combined with cyber capabilities or given extensive autonomy.
But super intelligence potentially changes the scale of the problem.
A system considerably more capable than humans across numerous cognitive domains could discover strategies, vulnerabilities and technological pathways at speeds beyond ordinary human comprehension.

If such capabilities were combined with recursive self-improvement, autonomous cyber operations or military command systems, humanity would be entering territory for which existing international law was never designed.
China’s concern should therefore become the basis for dialogue rather than suspicion.

The United States and China remain strategic competitors. They disagree profoundly over Taiwan, the South China Sea, technological controls, semiconductors and the future configuration of the Indo-Pacific.
Yet strategic competitors can recognise common existential risks.
The United States and Soviet Union did precisely this during the Cold War. Neither suddenly trusted the other.
Arms-control arrangements emerged because both eventually understood that unconstrained competition could produce mutual catastrophe.
AI requires similar maturity — except the international community may have considerably less time.
Unlike nuclear weapons, advanced AI systems can proliferate through software, computing networks, corporations, universities and research laboratories.
The barriers separating civilian and military applications can also be extremely thin.
This makes governance considerably more complicated.
Asean consequently has an important role.

Southeast Asia should not attempt to become merely an observer of an American-Chinese technological contest. Asean can help develop the diplomatic vocabulary necessary to distinguish legitimate AI development from dangerous military autonomy.

The Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting, ADMM-Plus, Asean Regional Forum and East Asia Summit provide platforms where principles of human control, transparency and crisis communication can gradually be developed.

Asean’s strength has never rested on coercive power. Its advantage lies in its capacity for circumscribed power: creating diplomatic spaces where countries that distrust one another can nevertheless continue talking.
This is precisely what AI governance requires.
Singapore has already emerged as an important location for discussions about military AI governance. Malaysia, Indonesia and other Asean members should reinforce these efforts.
The objective should not be an impossible attempt to stop AI.
It should be to establish internationally recognised guardrails before super intelligence becomes deeply integrated into military systems.
Human beings must retain meaningful authority over decisions involving lethal force. Nuclear command structures should never become dependent upon autonomous AI judgment.
Recursive self-improving systems must be subjected to stringent containment and testing.
Governments must also establish communication mechanisms capable of dealing with AI-related incidents before misunderstandings become military confrontations.
China’s warning at the Shangri-La Dialogue therefore deserves to be taken seriously.
It demonstrates that Beijing understands that technological supremacy becomes meaningless if the technology itself creates uncontrollable systemic dangers.
Washington should recognise the same reality.
The competition between China and the United States will continue. But there are areas where competition must be bounded by cooperation.
Super intelligence is one of them.
The mature strategic position is neither technological pessimism nor technological triumphalism.
It is recognition that humanity is developing increasingly powerful forms of intelligence without yet possessing equally powerful institutions to govern them.
China appears to understand this danger.
The United States does too.
The task now is to transform that shared anxiety into rules, communication channels and eventually international agreements before technological acceleration outruns diplomacy itself.
* Phar Kim Beng is professor of Asean Studies, and director at the Institute of International and Asean Studies, International Islamic University Malaysia.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
a9e70caad8f28839: TOKYO: Japan's real wages rose 1.5 per cent in August from a year earlier, marking the eighth consecutive month of gains, government data showed on Wednesday, pointing to a continued recovery in wage growth.
The solid wage data supports the case for the Bank of Japan to continue raising interest rates after hiking its benchmark rate last month.
The growth in real pay was slower than July's revised 2.0 per cent gain.
Average nominal wages, or total cash earnings, rose 3.8 per cent to 311,364 yen (US$1,969.66), slower than a revised 4.3 per cent increase in July.

Workers' base salaries, or regular pay, increased 3.8 per cent, unchanged from a revised 3.8 per cent rise in July. Overtime pay growth in August stood at 5.2 per cent, up from July's revised 4.5 per cent rise.
Special payments, consisting mostly of one-time bonuses that tend to be volatile, showed no growth in August after a revised 5.3 per cent increase in July.

The inflation rate used by the ministry to calculate the headline real wage indicator remained unchanged from July at 2.2 per cent. It remained below year-earlier levels, when it stood at 3.1 per cent.

Annual core inflation in Japan's capital accelerated in September at its fastest pace in 10 months, data showed last week, highlighting mounting price pressures and bolstering the case for further interest rate hikes from the central bank.
5e72ba49ac1a2f8b: WASHINGTON, Oct 7 — The female inmate who survived a failed execution in a US prison last week is now conscious and speaking, but her prognosis remains unclear, her lawyers said yesterday.
Christa Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death for a murder she committed when she was a teenager, received two supposedly lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital at a Tennessee prison a week ago.
She survived the injections, however, and was rushed to hospital, where she had been unconscious and on a ventilator in critical condition.
Pike’s lawyers said that “against all odds” she was now “conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care.”

“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” they said. “Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
Her lawyers repeated a call for Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
Lee suspended the carrying out of capital punishment in the southern state following the failed execution pending an independent investigation. The prison chief has resigned.
Pike’s case sparked debate over the death penalty for young offenders, as she was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp in 1995.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers sought clemency citing her age, childhood sexual abuse and mental health problems, including post-traumatic stress disorder.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, Pike is the first inmate ever to survive “after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs.” — AFP

486779719f3dd07b: PETALING JAYA, Oct 7 — For many, a trip to Bentong means indulging in all kinds of food the small town produces, including its yong tau foo.
In the Klang Valley, almost all the shops offer Hakka-style yong tau foo, where various beancurd items and vegetables are stuffed with fish paste or occasionally ground pork and salted fish.
Bentong does it differently; its residents are descendants of migrants from Guangxi, who use a mixture of fish paste, ground pork and Chinese chives.
The town is also famous for its tofu puffs with a distinct honeycomb interior, said to be prepared traditionally by cooking soybean milk over a firewood-fueled fire.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Long bean ‘yong tau foo’ (left) is exceptionally good with the studs of long beans stuck on the fish-pork paste. Bell pepper (right) is an unlikely partner for ‘yong tau foo’ but it works. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
When the paste and tofu puffs are combined, they become a powerhouse product marketed as Guangxi Tofu Puffs or even Bentong Tofu Puffs, which are sold frozen in packs.
With the opening of Da Jie Bentong about a month ago, there’s no need to drive up to Bentong for yong tau foo, as this family from Bentong has brought their family recipe to Kota Damansara.

Be warned: you may be tempted to order all 11 varieties of yong tau foo — chilli, eggplant, bitter gourd, tofu puff, lady’s finger, long bean, pork skin, beancurd, bell pepper, soup beancurd and white tofu — each priced at RM2.90.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Some of the ‘yong tau foo’ is served in a pork-chicken broth. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
I almost did because they looked so good but I eventually skipped a few since they weren’t my favourites.
These aren’t skinny yong tau foo on GLP-1 drugs but chunky bites that threaten your waistline.
Stuffed eggplant and bitter gourd passed their test with flying colours.
The eggplant was top-notch, featuring creamy flesh from a dip in hot oil, while the bitter gourd was cooked through without any raw bits.
The eye-opener was their long bean yong tau foo, as the paste wasn’t encased in the vegetable but was studded with chopped long beans!
It’s clever because you get the flavour and texture from the pan-fried long beans, which is a better match compared to those versions where the curled-up long beans feel disjointed when stuffed.
Now, bell pepper isn’t often found in yong tau foo places but perhaps they should use it as the vegetable has a soft, sweet flavour that matches the paste.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tofu puffs (left) are plump with the filling. Pig skin and the paste (right) are eaten like a sandwich. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Pork skin isn’t new to yong tau foo but this version sandwiches the chunky paste between the gelatinous skin, creating an unbeatable bite you’ll want more of.
And of course, there are the tofu puffs stuffed to the brim with paste, making a big bite which may be a struggle for some.
Those yong tau foo are served in a bowl of broth that has a light sweet flavour derived from pork and chicken bones.
You can pair your selected yong tau foo with rice, noodles or chee cheong fun.
Curry rules here, crafted from the family’s recipe using their homemade spice paste that is a Halloween orange colour that may spook you.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The Signature Curry Noodle is glorious in a striking orange, thick curry broth. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Their Signature Curry Noodle (RM15.90) is special too, featuring pan-fried long beans and creamy eggplant, rather than the half-cooked vegetables usually served with the noodles.
Even their Chee Cheong Fun (RM5) — flatter, silkier noodles with a thicker texture – is a fiery-sweet combination of curry sauce and sweet sauce.
They’re generous with the sauces; the dish is served in a bowl, ensuring every strand of the chee cheong fun is well coated.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Eat like the Bentong natives by combining your ‘chee cheong fun’ with curry and sweet sauce for a spicy-sweet flavour. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Even if you’re struggling to finish the food, remember to order their Signature Pepper Bun (RM10).
Back in Bentong, this was a popular order and after tasting that flaky meat-filled pastry, I also concur that it’s worthy of the fame.
It is inspired by the Taiwanese night market snack hujiaobing usually shaped like a bun but this version is longer.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Signature Pepper Bun (left) is dotted with toasted sesame seeds and filled with meat seasoned with pepper (right) and chopped scallions. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Bite it to get flaky pastry crusted with toasted sesame seeds and a juicy meat filling seasoned with pepper and chopped scallions.
If you’re not keen to drive to Kota Damansara, you can also get their food delivered to your doorstep with a tap, as the restaurant is on GrabFood.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Opened for a month plus, Da Jie Bentong is easily accessible at these shops within the Palm Spring development. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Restoran Da Jie Bentong
Lot B-G06, Palm Spring@Damansara,
Jalan PJU3/31,
Kota Damansara, Petaling Jaya.
Open: 11am to 9pm. Closed on Mondays.
* This is an independent review where the writer paid for the meal.

dbaf96d2d07674d5: KUALA LUMPUR: The Immigration Department will have access to real-time data sharing with multiple government agencies under the National Integrated Immigration System (NIISe), Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said.

He said NIISe would gradually replace the existing Malaysian Immigration System (myIMMs), with improvements including enhanced early screening, traveller risk profiling, and real-time data integration and sharing.

"These include the National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN), the police, Interpol, Inland Revenue Board (IRB), Prisons Department and Transport Ministry," he said in a written reply in response to a question from Rushdan Rusmi (PN-Padang Besar).
Saifuddin said the government currently implemented real-time data sharing and integration through myIMMs, an integrated information system supporting the Immigration Department's core operations.
He said myIMMs was used for immigration control and checks at the country's entry points, including checking travellers' or high-risk individuals' travel documents against Interpol databases.
"To modernise and improve the efficiency of control at entry points, improvements and modernisation of the system are continuously being implemented," he said.
He said the government was also developing the National Border Control System (SKSN) as a long-term plan to strengthen the country's border security ecosystem.

He said SKSN would be equipped with advanced surveillance systems based on artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to enable unmanned operations, rapid real-time information dissemination and continuous surveillance of Malaysia's land and maritime borders.
"The system is a plan by the ministry and efforts are still ongoing to refine its details," he said.

b13aeda92dd1e2d2: Coco Gauff said she was bombarded by an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media after winning a controversial point at the China Open on Monday in Beijing.

The US tennis star halted a first-set rally with 16-year-old Chinese hopeful Sun Xinran after the electronic advertising boards along the court flickered during play. After Sun appeared to win the point, the chair umpire ordered it to be replayed.
Gauff went on to win the third-round match 7-5, 6-1 against Sun, who won the US Open junior title this summer, but said she soon was inundated with racially charged comments.

"Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X. "The amount of racist comments/DMs I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Gauff explained in an Instagram post why she stopped playing the point.

"We are told before the matches we are allowed to continue to finish play so KEEP IT MIND I am thinking about all of this while I'm playing the point," she wrote. "Anything can be challenged after the point is over (as in most sports you can review a call after the play is over, I personally think is the correct rule). If I would've lost the point my opponent is also free to do the same thing and ask for a replay and she would've have been completely in her right to do so."

Gauff continued, "It was an unfortunate situation but it is out of my control, the think pieces and calling me an unfair (player) is ridiculous when those are the rules. I did not make them, I think it's weird I'm getting hate for following the rules. Xinran is incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood."
Sun was making her WTA Tour debut as a wild-card entry in the tournament. She appeared distraught following the loss to Gauff, 22, a two-time Grand Slam winner ranked No. 4 in the world.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career," Gauff said. "It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

cea089a5ba67fb27: Seventh-seeded Karolina Muchova outlasted 12th-seeded Naomi Osaka in their fourth-round match at the China Open on Tuesday in Beijing.

Muchova bounced back from a break down in both the first and third sets to post a 7-5, 1-6, 7-6 (7) victory. The Czech recorded four aces and 52 winners to offset 50 unforced errors and dispatched the Japan native in 2 hours and 52 minutes.
Muchova was unable to convert triple-match point at 5-4 in the third set, as well as three other match points in the ensuing tiebreaker before winning the ninth on a backhand volley.

"I honestly didn't even believe I will finish the match," Muchova said in her on-court interview. "So many match points, I didn't know how many. After a match point I was like, 'OK, I'm going for it,' but then I think she always played great and steady, and didn't make mistakes – unlike me, unfortunately! I was shaking. I'm happy that I made the last volley and it was really so close. Naomi could be standing here. It's me, and I'm really grateful for it."
Osaka struck 11 aces and converted five of 10 break-point opportunities.

Muchova, 30, advanced to the quarterfinals to set up a maiden matchup against countrywoman Nikola Bartunkova. The 20-year-old Bartunkova followed up her upset of Aryna Sabalenka with a 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 victory over Sinja Kraus of Austria.

"It's been an unbelievable year for me," Bartunkova said after the 1-hour, 46-minute match. "I didn't expect before this year that I play like this and I will be here. It's great, but just now I focus on myself, improve my game because it's still 50-50 every match.
"I'm still young, so I need to have more experience and this is my goal now."
No. 19 seed Ekaterina Alexandrova of Russia breezed to a 6-2, 6-2 victory over Czech Linda Noskova, the tournament's fifth seed.
Noskova committed six double faults on her way to the lopsided loss.
Alexandrova advanced to face fourth-seeded Russian Mirra Andreeva, who coasted to a 6-2, 6-2 win over Ukraine's Daria Snigur.
56017bed48f3a4c7: KOTA BARU: A man was killed when the four-wheel-drive (4WD) vehicle he was driving skidded before plunging into a ravine about 100m deep at Jalan Ladang Pos Pulat in Gua Musang.
The vehicle and victim were found two days after the incident.

Gua Musang police chief superintendent Sik Choon Foo said police received a report from the public at 4.30pm yesterday about the discovery of the Toyota Hilux at the bottom of the ravine, with the victim found unconscious and pronounced dead at the scene.
He said preliminary investigations found that the accident was believed to have occurred on Sunday.
"Based on information from the victim's wife, the victim's last live location was detected on Sunday afternoon in the vicinity of the incident.
"On Oct 6, the victim's colleague went to the location of the last live location to search for him before finding the victim's Toyota Hilux at the bottom of the ravine," he said in a statement today.
Sik said investigations found that the victim was believed to have been driving his vehicle when it skidded into the ravine while going downhill.
He said no one was believed to have witnessed the incident, resulting in the vehicle driven by the victim going unnoticed by members of the public until it was found by his colleague.

The victim's body was subsequently brought up from the scene with the assistance of personnel from the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department before being sent to the Forensic Unit of Gua Musang Hospital for a post-mortem.
"The case is being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987 for the offence of reckless or dangerous driving resulting in death.
"Further investigations are still being conducted to identify the actual cause of the accident and the circumstances that led to the incident," he said.

e3238eb49d3b9501: KUALA LUMPUR: The government has dropped the proposal to establish the National Harmony Commission (SKN), National Unity Minister Datuk Aaron Ago Dagang said.

Aaron said the ministry would instead focus on strengthening existing institutions, namely the National Unity and Integration Department, Rukun Tetangga and community mediators, as the lead agencies in managing social harmony.

He said the decision was made after the National Unity Ministry conducted two engagement sessions involving civil society organisations, government agencies, academics, community leaders and other stakeholders to assess the need, scope, implications, challenges and feasibility of establishing the commission.
"After taking into account the views of all parties and further consideration, the ministry has decided not to proceed with the establishment of SKN as a new entity.
"This is as discussed and decided at the first 2026 meeting of the National Unity Advisory Council (MPPN).

"This also avoids duplication of functions and the cost of establishing a new entity, while making use of the existing structures, networks and instruments developed by JPNIN," he said in a written parliamentary reply.

He was responding to a question from Dr V. Sivakumar (PH-Batu Gajah), who asked about the status and timeline for establishing the commission, its proposed enforcement powers and assurances that it would not overlap with existing agencies dealing with discrimination and racial tensions.
In April, the government was reviving the plan to establish SKN, with the National Unity Ministry backing a renewed proposal amid growing concerns over unity-related issues.

It was said that the move followed a proposal by activist Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye and built on earlier efforts dating back to 2015, when the National Unity Advisory Council drafted three bills on racial and religious hatred offences, national harmony and reconciliation, and the establishment of a commission.
However, in 2019, the government rejected two of the bills due to overlaps with existing laws and constitutional provisions, including Article 8 of the Federal Constitution on non-discrimination.
bed5054866bfd9df: REYKJAVIK: Russia should share more information about the death of a plague laboratory worker who died last week, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Tuesday, in an incident Washington was watching "very closely".

A laboratory worker at Siberia's plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on Friday, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of ‌people and sparking public health fears on social media.
Russian authorities have said the situation is under control.
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio told reporters in Iceland. "We're watching it very closely, hour by hour."
Rubio said the US has measures available to help Russia if the situation turns out to be more serious than has so far been acknowledged, but needed to know more before it could step in.

a8267a3359ee9044: BURNING, tingling or numb feet can be easy to dismiss, but for people with diabetes, they may signal changes in the nerves.
A burning sensation that appears as you settle into bed. A prickling feeling that comes and goes.
Numbness that's difficult to put into words… For someone living with diabetes, such changes can be easy to dismiss, especially when there's no actual pain.
But sometimes, what the feet are telling you deserves closer attention.
These sensations can be among the signs of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, a form of nerve damage associated with diabetes that commonly affects the feet and legs.
And because nerve damage can also reduce sensation, the absence of pain doesn't necessarily mean everything's fine.
A recently published Malaysian study on neuropathic pain (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com) offers a glimpse of how relevant the issue may be locally.
Among 13,592 adults screened across nine tertiary hospitals, 40.1 per cent of those who reported having diabetes screened positive for probable neuropathic pain.
The result was a screening finding, not a diagnosis, and didn't establish that diabetes was the cause.
But it does underline why unusual or persistent sensations are worth discussing with a healthcare professional.
RECOGNISE THE UNFAMILIAR
The difficulty, says Dr Tan Kenny, consultant neurologist at Loh Guan Lye Specialists Centre (LSC), is that people don't necessarily describe nerve-related symptoms as pain.
"They don't always use the word 'pain' when describing what they feel. They may say their feet feel hot, prickly or strangely numb."
That distinction matters.
One person may experience a burning or shooting sensation, sometimes more noticeable at night.
Another may notice pins and needles or a gradual loss of feeling. Someone else may have little or no obvious symptoms at all.
And while diabetes can be associated with nerve damage, it shouldn't automatically be assumed to be the explanation for every episode of tingling or numbness.
"Having diabetes doesn't automatically explain every episode of tingling, so we need to understand the symptoms, examine the patient and consider other possible causes," advises Dr Tan Kenny.
That's why noticing a change – rather than trying to work out its cause yourself – is often the more useful first step.

There's another reason not to ignore a gradual loss of sensation. When feeling in the feet is reduced, a blister, cut or other injury may be harder to notice. Something that would normally hurt enough to demand attention may go unnoticed instead.
In other words, not hurting doesn't necessarily mean nothing is wrong.
WHAT YOUR FEET ARE TELLING YOU
Before seeing a healthcare professional, it helps to pay attention to what has actually changed.
Does it feel like burning, prickling or an electric shock? Does the numbness affect one foot or both?
When did it begin, and is it becoming more frequent or noticeable?
It's also useful to consider whether it's affecting sleep, walking or other everyday activities, and whether there are visible changes such as a wound, redness or swelling.
These observations are not a diagnostic test; they simply give a healthcare professional a clearer picture of what's happening.

For those unsure how to describe what they're experiencing, a six-question digital neuropathic pain screening tool developed by Viatris Malaysia (https://www.painscreeningtool.com/) offers another starting point.
It's designed to help users describe the type of pain they're experiencing to a healthcare professional.
Even without symptoms, routine foot assessments remain an important part of diabetes care.
"Pain tends to get our attention, but a gradual loss of feeling can be easier to overlook," says Dr Fang Li Chen, consultant physician at LSC.
"Foot health should be part of regular diabetes reviews. Patients should check their feet daily and seek medical advice promptly for a new wound, redness or swelling - even if it doesn't hurt."
BEYOND THE SYMPTOM
If nerve-related symptoms are raised during a consultation, assessment typically begins with a review of the symptoms and medical history, followed by checks of the feet, sensation and circulation.
Further tests or specialist referral depend on the findings.
For patients, the first step is simply to tell their healthcare professional what feels different. Where further expertise is needed, care may involve different disciplines.
The appropriate combination of care depends on the individual's symptoms and clinical findings.
It's advisable to consult a healthcare professional to ensure you have all the necessary information and guidance before making any healthcare decisions.
WHEN PAIN AFFECTS LIFE
For those experiencing nerve pain, the problem may extend beyond the sensation itself.
Persistent discomfort can interfere with sleep. Changes in how the feet feel may affect walking or other activities.
And when a symptom begins to alter the way someone goes about an ordinary day, that's useful information for a healthcare professional to know.

"A pain score tells us only part of the story. We also want to understand how symptoms affect sleep, movement and everyday life," says Dr Chan Wei Heng, consultant orthopaedic surgeon and Interventional Pain specialist at LSC, adding: "When patients have overlapping pain or mobility concerns, working alongside colleagues involved in diabetes and nerve care allows us to look at the patient more holistically and ensure the appropriate specialist assessment and care are considered."
It's a reminder that managing nerve pain is about more than reducing a number on a pain scale.
It's also about helping someone sleep more comfortably, move with confidence and get on with everyday life.
For someone living with diabetes, the most useful habit is also the simplest: paying attention to what has changed.
It could be a burning foot at bedtime, or persistent pins and needles. An unfamiliar patch of numbness, or a small wound that has gone unnoticed.
None of these symptoms, on its own, tells you exactly what's happening. But they may be worth talking about.
Sometimes, noticing the difference is the first step towards finding out why.
For info regarding clinical services available at Loh Guan Lye Specialists Centre, go to www.lohguanlye.com.

c84a52c53f2a10c0: ENTERTAINER Datuk Leonard Tan, known as the "Singer with a Thousand Voices" and "King of Jingles", is one of Malaysia's most sought-after performers.
The singer, actor and comedian performs at corporate functions nationwide.
Tan is famous for impersonating stars like Louis Armstrong, the Bee Gees and Tan Sri P. Ramlee.
Drawing energy from his audiences, Tan delivers lively performances that keep crowds entertained.
Tan has provided vocals for commercial jingles for brands including KFC, A&W, Gardenia, McDonald's and Proton.
Tan is known for his charity work, having performed at numerous fund-raising events.
"My wish is for Malaysians to remember those in need and do something to improve their lives," Tan said in an interview.
"I've always had a passion for music and creativity. In fact, I was one of the founding members of the Positive Tone record label in the 1990s.
"This label helped launch many talents who later became household names.
"I wasn't just a singer. I produced my own albums, including 'Bintang Bukannya Satu', 'Leonard Tan', and 'Christmas with Leonard'."
In 2004, Tan made his film debut in 'Ah Lok Kafe', an English-language Malaysian film based on an original story by cartoonist Reggie Lee and directed by Anwardi Jamil.
Tan played the title character, Ah Lok.
"Playing an honest-to-goodness Malaysian Elvis Presley gave audiences a proper laugh."
Tan grew up in Penang as one of nine siblings in a musically gifted family.
"My eldest brother was in a very popular band called The Thunderbolts, famous for their track 'Thunderbolt Twist'.
"My siblings gave me tremendous encouragement to develop my own style."
EARLY DAYS AND MUSICAL INFLUENCES
Tan's earliest musical influences included rock acts such as Bachman-Turner Overdrive, Electric Light Orchestra, The Sweet and Osibisa, as well as jazz and Motown classics.
Locally, he drew inspiration from groups such as Sweet September, Carefree, Discovery and Black Dog Bone.
Although Tan began singing at school and dreamt of becoming a performer, music wasn't his only ambition.
"I also wanted to become a hotelier. So, after saving money from odd jobs and gigs, I went to Canada to pursue my studies."
One of Tan's fondest memories was competing in the 1980s Top of the Pubs contest, shortly after he moved from Penang to Kuala Lumpur.
"I had just moved to KL and barely had any friends or supporters. Only two friends came up to wish me luck that night. That's why I cherish that memory."
Tan credits Kenny Tay of pop-rock trio Kenny, Remy & Martin as the most inspiring musician he has ever met.
"Kenny discovered me, and together we produced my Malay album, 'Bintang Bukannya Satu'. I'm grateful to him, and we've remained friends all these years."
BUILDING A FAN BASE
Tan credits early television appearances with building his fan base.
"I appeared regularly on Radio Televisyen Malaysia, which gave me tremendous exposure.
"It helped me establish a fan base in Sabah, Sarawak and Labuan, leading to invitations to perform there.
"From there, I starred in 'Ah Lok Kafe' and even a Hong Kong comedy flick.
"I have wonderful memories of working alongside brilliant filmmakers and performers throughout the 1990s and 2000s."
After performing at venues across the country, Tan recently ticked another venue off his bucket list: Unifi Arena in Bukit Jalil.
"The best thing about the arena is its state-of-the-art sound system and accessibility, making it a favourite spot for concertgoers."
Looking ahead, Tan hopes to collaborate with Lionel Richie and Sir Elton John.
"They are phenomenal performers. I grew up watching their concerts on television.
"Despite being superstars, they are humble, down-to-earth and gracious with their fans. It is my dream to meet and collaborate with them."
Tan sings in English, Malay, Chinese and other languages.
Next on his list is learning a language from Sabah and Sarawak.
"I believe that as a Malaysian, mastering our country's languages is a goal worth striving for."
LESSONS LEARNED AND HIDDEN TALENTS
Despite decades of experience, he said he still gets nervous before stepping onstage.
"I've even tripped on stage twice," he said with a smile.
"The backstage area was pitch-black, causing me to miss the steps leading to the stage. To make matters worse, the connecting ladder was unstable.
"But that's life. Everyone encounters a mishap now and then.
"In hindsight, it was quite funny. I turned it into a joke and the audience went wild with laughter. Falling turned out to be a great learning process."
Had he not pursued entertainment, he believes he might have become a police officer or hotelier.
"I have keen detective instincts, which would make me a good cop.
"As an actor, I love playing diverse roles. And I enjoy hospitality, so being a hotelier would have been a natural fit."
He added that he briefly harboured dreams of becoming a doctor, though financial constraints made that path impractical.
His friends also regard cooking as one of his hidden talents.
"Everyone tells me my hidden talent is cooking. Plus, I used to be a track and rally driver."
On Oct 10, Tan will perform at the "MfM Benefit Showcase: Rocking for a Cause" at Kelab Golf Negara Subang in Petaling Jaya.
Organised by Musicians for Musicians (MfM), the event supports Malaysian musicians.

0f68436416fa7720: PETALING JAYA: Pooling medicine purchases across Asean could lower costs and strengthen Malaysia’s resilience against supply disruptions, a pharmacy expert said.

Malaysian Pharmacists Society (MPS) president Amrahi Buang said that the strategy could be especially beneficial for high-cost medicines and orphan drugs for rare diseases, since small patient populations tend to limit the bargaining power of individual countries.
“Consolidating demand across Asean member states creates larger order volumes, allowing countries to negotiate steeper discounts from pharmaceutical manufacturers,” he told FMT.

He said combining the demand for rare-disease treatments could turn small national markets into more commercially attractive regional contracts, improving the prospects of securing affordable supplies.
Amrahi was commenting on plans outlined by health minister Dzulkefly Ahmad for Malaysia to co-lead a regional medicine procurement framework with the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
Work on the framework and financing mechanism is scheduled for 2027–2028, with a pilot targeted by 2030.

Amrahi said the pooled procurement of 82 medicines for healthcare facilities run by the health, defence and higher education ministries helped the country achieve an estimated RM179.6 million, or 17.7% in savings.
The health ministry study, which compared contracts for 2018–2020 and 2020–2022, found that switching from original-brand medicines to generics had also contributed to the savings.
“Malaysia’s domestic success strongly indicates that expanding to a regional Asean model could yield even greater benefits, but it requires navigating different pricing dynamics,” said Amrahi.
He said a larger purchasing pool could provide additional leverage when negotiating for patented and rare-disease medicines without generic alternatives.

Beyond prices, Amrahi said regional cooperation could support coordinated stockpiling and access to a wider network of manufacturers, helping countries withstand disruptions and reduce dependence on individual suppliers.
However, he said regional savings would vary according to the medicines purchased, countries’ economic capacities and differences in regulatory requirements.
For the mechanism to work, he said participating countries would need reliable demand forecasts, common product specifications, transparent pricing and guaranteed purchase volumes.

The procurement initiative forms part of the Asean drug security and self-reliance action plan under the Asean Strategic Health Agenda 2026–2030, launched at the 17th Asean Health Ministers Meeting in Kuala Lumpur in September.
7cf400fdd354d2c1: PETALING JAYA: Perolehan ubat secara bersama dalam kalangan negara Asean boleh mengurangkan kos dan pada masa sama memperkukuh daya tahan Malaysia dalam menghadapi gangguan bekalan, kata seorang pakar farmasi.

Presiden Persatuan Farmasi Malaysia (MPS) Amrahi Buang berkata pendekatan itu boleh memberi manfaat khususnya bagi ubat berharga tinggi dan ubat untuk penyakit jarang berlaku kerana jumlah pesakit yang kecil biasanya mengehadkan kuasa tawar-menawar sesebuah negara.

“Apabila permintaan daripada negara anggota Asean digabungkan, jumlah tempahan menjadi lebih besar dan ini membolehkan negara berunding untuk mendapatkan diskaun lebih tinggi daripada pengeluar farmaseutikal,” katanya kepada FMT.

Beliau berkata penggabungan permintaan bagi rawatan penyakit jarang berlaku juga boleh menjadikan pasaran kecil di setiap negara lebih menarik dari sudut komersial apabila ditawarkan sebagai kontrak serantau, sekali gus meningkatkan peluang mendapatkan bekalan pada harga berpatutan.
Amrahi mengulas rancangan diumumkan Menteri Kesihatan Dzulkefly Ahmad supaya Malaysia bersama Filipina, Singapura dan Thailand menerajui pembangunan kerangka perolehan ubat serantau.
Pembangunan kerangka dan mekanisme pembiayaan itu dijadualkan pada 2027 hingga 2028, manakala projek rintis disasarkan dilaksanakan menjelang 2030.

Amrahi berkata perolehan bersama 82 jenis ubat untuk kemudahan kesihatan di bawah kementerian kesihatan, pertahanan dan pendidikan tinggi membantu negara mencatat anggaran penjimatan RM179.6 juta atau 17.7%.

Kajian Kementerian Kesihatan yang membandingkan kontrak bagi tempoh 2018 hingga 2020 dan 2020 hingga 2022 turut mendapati penggunaan ubat generik menggantikan ubat jenama asal menyumbang kepada penjimatan berkenaan.
“Kejayaan Malaysia di peringkat domestik menunjukkan model serantau Asean berpotensi memberi manfaat lebih besar, tetapi perbezaan dalam struktur harga perlu diuruskan dengan baik,” katanya.

Beliau berkata kumpulan pembelian yang lebih besar juga boleh memberi kuasa tawar-menawar tambahan dalam rundingan bagi ubat berpaten dan rawatan penyakit jarang berlaku yang tidak mempunyai alternatif generik.

Selain harga, Amrahi berkata kerjasama serantau boleh membolehkan penyelarasan stok simpanan dan akses kepada rangkaian pengeluar lebih luas, sekali gus membantu negara menghadapi gangguan bekalan serta mengurangkan kebergantungan kepada pembekal tertentu.
Bagaimanapun, beliau berkata kadar penjimatan di peringkat serantau mungkin berbeza bergantung kepada jenis ubat, kemampuan ekonomi setiap negara serta perbezaan keperluan kawal selia.
Menurutnya, mekanisme itu memerlukan unjuran permintaan yang tepat, spesifikasi produk yang seragam, harga yang telus dan jaminan jumlah pembelian daripada negara yang mengambil bahagian.

Inisiatif perolehan itu adalah sebahagian daripada pelan tindakan keselamatan dan kebergantungan kendiri ubat Asean di bawah Agenda Strategik Kesihatan Asean 2026-2030 yang dilancarkan pada Mesyuarat menteri-menteri Kesihatan Asean ke-17 di Kuala Lumpur pada September.
55cc78ed0fcff389: PETALING JAYA: For many older adults, taking glucosamine is part of a daily routine to ease aching joints. But research suggests this familiar supplement deserves closer attention when someone also has problems with memory and thinking.

Scientists at the University of Florida found that glucosamine use was associated with a higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Published in Nature Metabolism, the study analysed patient records alongside experiments involving mice and donated human brain tissue.

The findings raise questions about whether a supplement taken for one health concern could have unintended effects elsewhere. However, they do not establish that glucosamine causes dementia or worsens it in humans.

Mild cognitive impairment describes memory or thinking difficulties beyond those expected with normal ageing, while everyday independence remains largely intact. Researchers examined health records from 2012 to 2024, comparing patients with recorded glucosamine use and those without.

After accounting for factors including age and sex, they found a 25% higher likelihood of progression to dementia among glucosamine users with mild cognitive impairment. This was an increase relative to non-users, not a finding that 25% of everyone taking the supplement would develop dementia.

Among patients already diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias, glucosamine use was also associated with a 25% higher risk of death during follow-up. The same link was not observed in the mild cognitive impairment group.

Differences in health, lifestyle or other characteristics between users and non-users could have influenced the findings, even after statistical adjustments. Study co-author Matt Gentry, who chairs the university’s department of biochemistry and molecular biology, stressed the need for further investigation.

“While it’s an association and not proof of causality, it does raise an important clinical question that now deserves much more attention,” he said. The team also explored a possible explanation in the laboratory.

Glucosamine occurs naturally in the body and can cross the protective barrier between the bloodstream and the brain. It helps fuel a process that attaches sugar structures to proteins, allowing them to take the right shape, reach the right places and work properly.

These tiny “tags” are part of normal cell function, but the researchers found evidence that this system becomes overactive in Alzheimer’s disease. Donated brain tissue from people with Alzheimer’s showed more of these structures than tissue from people without the disease.

In mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s-like features, glucosamine worsened their ability to recognise animals they had encountered before. Reducing activity in the sugar-building process, meanwhile, improved memory performance.

Together, these findings suggest that changes in how brain cells process these molecules could contribute to the disease. However, results in mice cannot establish what a supplement will do in people.
So, what does this mean for supplement users?
A brain already affected by disease may respond differently to glucosamine from a healthy one. Human clinical trials are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about its effects.
For now, the study does not show that everyone taking glucosamine faces an increased dementia risk. Nor does it establish that stopping the supplement will slow cognitive decline.
People with diagnosed cognitive impairment or dementia who take glucosamine can discuss the findings with their doctor or pharmacist when reviewing their medicines and supplements.

eed6829551537c90: MELAKA: The Election Commission (EC) will hold a special meeting today to fix the key dates for the 16th Melaka state election.
The meeting will be chaired by EC chairman Datuk Seri Ramlan Harun, followed by a press conference scheduled at 11.30am to announce the decisions.
Among the matters to be determined are the election writ date, nomination day, early voting day and polling day, as well as the electoral roll.
The election arrangements are also expected to include the use of nomination centres and polling centres, as well as preparations for election personnel to ensure the voting process runs smoothly.
The dissolution of the state assembly on Sept 23 paved the way for an election to be held within 60 days.

With 28 seats up for contest, the state election will not only determine who forms the state government but will also be an important test of the actual strength of political blocs following major changes to the national political landscape since the 2021 Melaka state election.
In terms of voter numbers, Melaka is now vastly different from the state election five years ago.
As at April 20, 2026, the number of registered voters in Melaka stood at 683,543, an increase of 188,348, or about 38 per cent, from the 495,195 voters in the 2021 state election.
The addition of nearly 190,000 voters means this state election has a different demographic dimension.
New voters, including those automatically registered following the implementation of Undi18, could be a determining factor, particularly in seats previously won by narrow majorities.
The figure could also change further when the EC finalises the electoral roll.

The August 2026 Supplementary Electoral Roll alone contains 43,309 citizens aged 18 and above who were automatically registered as new voters, in addition to 34,411 voters who changed their constituencies and 2,728 who changed their voter category or status.
It will not only determine the overall number of voters but also provide a clearer picture of the size of the electoral field each party will face across the 28 state constituencies.
In the 2021 polls, BN won 21 state seats, while five were won by Pakatan Harapan (PH) and two by Perikatan Nasional (PN).
17f760c0018852de: BUENOS AIRES: An emotional Lionel Messi prepared to bring the curtain down on his glittering 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in a friendly against Benin.
Messi, 39, was seen wiping away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina team-mates made its way through crowds of wellwishers en route to a sold out Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires.

Shortly before kick off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word "Gracias" (Thank You) above the football superstar's No 10 was laid out on the pitch as a sellout crowd of 85,000 roared their approval.
Messi was seen welling up once again moments before kick-off in a stirring rendition of Argentina's national anthem.
Tuesday's fixture has been billed as 'The Last Tango', a chance to pay tribute to the diminutive genius widely regarded as the greatest player in football history.
Messi announced his retirement from international football in August, ending an Argentina career that spanned more than two decades, encompassed 207 matches and a record 125 goals.
His farewell comes two and a half months after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.
"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote at the time.
Before Tuesday's game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.
Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.
"To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!," he joked.
Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed "The joy of my life."
Former Barcelona teammate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.
"It's not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more," he said.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
Filling the void
Several of his fellow 2022 World Cup champions will participate in the tribute, including Angel di Maria, who has already retired from the national team.
Messi will wear a commemorative jersey with a white stripe down the centre and the sun's rays from the national flag.
The city of Buenos Aires will light up its main monuments in light blue, including the iconic Obelisk.
"It's going to be an unforgettable day for everyone," coach Lionel Scaloni said in the build-up to Tuesday's match.
Vice-captain, defender Nicolas Otamendi, will also bow out of the team on Tuesday as Messi signs off.

Messi's departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country's 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona's heir.

"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.
During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.
But there were tears along the way too, with Messi retiring for two months from the team after their shock defeat on penalties to Chile in the 2016 Copa America final.
After the Benin game, the captain's armband will pass to Cristian Romero.
It is not clear, however, who will inherit the coveted number 10 jersey.
"Until Leo's game, we won't give the number 10 to anyone," said Scaloni. "After that, we'll see."
177cca44c3046141: WASHINGTON: A lawyer for Walt Disney urged a US judge on Tuesday to block the Federal Communications Commission's early review of licences for its eight company-owned ABC TV stations, saying President Donald Trump's administration is seeking to censor and punish the company for airing content it does not like.

The company's lawsuit, filed in August, poses a key test for the free speech rights of broadcasters under the US Constitution's First Amendment versus the Trump administration's efforts to reshape the media landscape.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programmes he dislikes or which have joked about or criticised him or his administration. The Republican president has also repeatedly called on the FCC to strip stations of licences after criticising news and other programming.
The First Amendment protects against government abridgment of free speech.

"Our concern is that we are chilled. We are making different editorial decisions," Disney lawyer Beth Wilkinson told US District Judge Loren AliKhan during a hearing in the company's suit seeking to block the unusual early FCC licence reviews, comparing ABC's fate to being under a guillotine during the French Revolution.

"We are watching everything that we do because every time we do something — even not broadcasting this presidential speech — brings out the anger in the administration and the retaliation from the agency," Wilkinson said.

Wilkinson was referring to ABC's decision not to carry a live broadcast of a July 16 speech in which Trump revived his long-running attacks on US election security. Trump for years has made false claims of widespread US voting fraud. Comcast-owned NBC also did not broadcast Trump's speech live. Afterward, Trump called for both to lose their licences.
Profitable stations

FCC Chair Brendan Carr ordered the early reviews of the ABC stations in April. The licences for the eight stations — including some of Disney's most profitable ones in cities including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Houston — were not due to expire until 2028 to 2031. Carr said last week that he has made no decisions on how to proceed.

Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel, a lawyer for the administration, said the guillotine analogy was misplaced, noting that Disney in any circumstance would retain its ABC licences through the administrative process and judicial review.
AliKhan previously declined to bar the FCC from issuing an order to refer the licences for a public hearing. The FCC has agreed to provide at least 48 hours' notice to the court before moving ahead.
The judge held the two-hour-long hearing to help determine whether she should issue a preliminary injunction, as Disney has requested, to block the FCC's action.

Carr opened an investigation in March 2025 into Disney's diversity practices and said the company submitted documents he viewed as insufficient. Carr has said the early licence renewal review was prompted by Disney's failure to quickly respond to those document requests.
During the hearing, AliKhan cited earlier comments by Trump and Carr, and questioned the administration's argument "that this is merely over a discovery dispute," referring to producing documents.

"I imagine we have a lot of discovery disputes with a lot of your licensees," the judge told Georgiev-Remmel. "So what is it that made this so different that you needed to call for an early licence renewal?"

The administration argued that Disney's suit should have been filed in a federal appeals court and that the company should have appealed the FCC staff order to review its licences before filing the lawsuit.
The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before it did so in this instance.
The licence reviews were ordered a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations are extremely rare, critics say threats of losing a licence can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in programming decisions.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show "The View," which discusses politics, after saying it may be subject to federal rules requiring broadcasters to provide equal opportunities to political candidates. Disney noted that since February, the programme has not invited any political candidates to appear, citing the FCC's "pressure campaign".

Last month, Kimmel said FCC threats prevented the airing of his interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico during a broadcast. The interview was instead posted on YouTube, where it has been viewed more than 13 million times.

b82e3cb67f14e299: LOS ANGELES: Paramount on Tuesday completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting two of Hollywood's most storied studios in a media empire spanning television, news and cinema under the control of David Ellison.

Ellison plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, while a company memo warned that layoffs could be in store.
His ultra-wealthy family's ties to US President Donald Trump have raised concerns among critics that the new Hollywood giant will toe the White House line in its news coverage.
"It's going to be a great company," Trump told reporters Tuesday as he left the White House.
Layoffs loom

The sprawling new corporation faces considerable challenges, with the entertainment industry in flux as streaming services and YouTube draw viewers away from traditional TV and movie theatre audiences dwindle.
Skydance shares ended their first day trading down 2.7 per cent on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker "SKYD."
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

Paramount won a bidding war against Netflix in February for Warner Bros. Discovery, and the Trump administration approved the deal, one of the largest-ever media mergers, in June without demanding a change to its business.
Skydance, which will have nearly US$70 billion in annual revenue, said it is targeting more than US$6 billion in cost savings within three years.
Ellison will serve as chairman and chief executive officer, with former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations and integrating the two businesses.
In a memo to the company's staff, titled "Day 1," Ellison and Kreiz said the merger "will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce."
"We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully," said the memo seen by AFP.
The deal was backed by US$47 billion in new equity led by the Ellison family, private equity firm RedBird Capital and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
Ellison's father, billionaire Oracle founder Larry Ellison, provided major funding and a guarantee to lenders backing the deal.
The Ellison family holds the largest equity stake in Skydance.

Opponents in the movie industry said the combined company would slash jobs in a Hollywood already under pressure and reduce the number of films produced every year, while news media groups feared CNN's independence could be compromised.
The settlement with the states includes several safeguards on these issues, including a board meant to protect CNN's editorial independence.

481d34a929323087: SEOUL: North Korea criticised the United States over its arms sales and military support for Taiwan, accusing Washington of fuelling tensions in the Taiwan Strait, state media KCNA said on Wednesday.

2cc59d0974085215: WASHINGTON: The female inmate who survived a failed execution in a US prison last week is now conscious and speaking, but her prognosis remains unclear, her lawyers said Tuesday.

284766f4b52ea2bf: JOHOR BAHRU: PKR MP Hassan Karim has urged the four former MPs who have quit the party to stop their persistent personal attacks on Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and PKR.

a8b6b0f58ad98735: JOHOR BAHRU: Ahli Parlimen PKR Hassan Karim menggesa empat bekas Ahli Parlimen yang meninggalkan parti itu supaya menghentikan serangan peribadi berterusan terhadap Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim dan PKR.

553304f8227cd6ab: KANGAR: When Jamaludin Abd Rahman first looked at the muddy patch of land in Kampung Bunga Emas Barat, it was hardly promising farmland. The 0.3ha site had been left largely unused because its soil was deep, unstable and difficult to work.
“Previously, this was abandoned swamp land. If you walked through it, you could easily sink into the mud, so machinery such as tractors and rice harvesters could not enter,” the 63-year-old recalled.
Jamaludin, who hails from Jerlun, Kedah, initially dug a pond there to rear catfish. But he began thinking more seriously about what the land could support.
“After considering the potential of the land, I decided to gradually plant about 1,000 nipah palms,” he told Bernama.
That was in 2019. Today, the plantation has expanded to more than 5,000 palms, giving the father of six a way to work with the swamp rather than against it.
Nipah, however, demands patience. Jamaludin said the palms take about five years to mature before they begin producing sap, and extracting that sap relies on skills that are increasingly unfamiliar.
The process involves carefully preparing the stalks through traditional techniques that include twisting, wrapping and tapping them at particular intervals and rhythms.
Done properly, the sweet liquid slowly drips into collection bags or containers.
“Many people assume that the rainy season produces more sap, but in fact, nipah sap flows more abundantly and tastes richer and better during the dry season,” Jamaludin revealed.
The palm’s deep root system allows it to draw water from underground even when the surface soil dries out, helping the plant thrive in conditions that might prove difficult for other crops.
For Jamaludin, who is also an artist, the plantation has gradually become more than a source of sap: he sees it as a way of preserving a landscape and the older practices associated with it.

Nipah palms can help stabilise muddy soil, reduce erosion and act as a natural buffer when water levels rise. Their leaves, meanwhile, have long been used by villagers for traditional roofing and leaf-wrapped cigarettes.
That connection between plant, place and custom now forms part of what visitors experience at Nipah Klasik, the family-run eatery built around the plantation.

Fresh sap is served for consumption alongside local favourites such as popiah, keropok lekor and fish otak-otak, while visitors can eat among the palms and watch demonstrations of how the sap is collected.
For Jamaludin, the setting also offers a chance to show how a landscape once dismissed as unusable can support food, livelihoods and traditional knowledge.
Rather than forcing the land into conventional agriculture, he has found a use that suits its character.

And in doing so, a once-difficult stretch of swamp has become a place where people can taste something local, learn how it is made, and spend a little time among the plants that made the transformation possible.

05d3df235348daa8: LOS ANGELES: President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans.

Trump, speaking at a political rally in the state's farm belt on Monday, discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to "see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did."

"And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial, it's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay," he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertiliser and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war.

"It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it's going to be over with very soon," he said.
"It's essentially almost over with," Trump went on. "But it's going to end very soon, and it's going to end one way or the other."

On Tuesday, the White House dismissed criticism of the remark. "The media freakout over President Trump's comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung said in a social media post. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."

Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil.
Early voting underway in California

The comment in rural Nebraska, a state Trump won with more than 55 per cent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run cities in California, a solidly Democratic state the president often criticises.
Monday's comments prompted a backlash from California officials.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, denounced the Republican president as "deranged and dangerous".
"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," he wrote on X.

Newsom, who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, juxtaposed a video clip of Trump in Nebraska with mention of the president's previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration.

California's early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday. The president's Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state in recent years, including this year's gubernatorial election.

Newsom championed the redrawing of California's congressional map last year to favour Democrats in this year's election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to redraw its map to boost Republicans.
One of the Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from Trump's remarks.

"I vehemently disagree with President Trump's comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," he wrote on X. "No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage."

US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump's comment was "unhelpful".
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump's comment "could potentially compromise our safety".
Appearing on MS Now on Tuesday, Bass disputed Cheung's assertion that Trump's comments were being misinterpreted by a "freaked out" media.

"Well, I'm not sure that he understands that we can hear what the president said," Bass countered, adding that Cheung's defence of Trump's remarks "has no connection to the words that came out of the president's mouth."
Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population.
More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego, including Naval Base San Diego, the largest on the US west coast.

"My constituents — including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families — are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump's stupid war," US Representative Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post.

61bc600f4b2ce6b5: MEXICO CITY: From former and current team mates to tearful fans outside the Monumental stadium, tributes poured in for Argentine great Lionel Messi on Tuesday as the country prepared to bid farewell to their captain in his final international appearance.

Before the final goodbye, he offered a simple message of his own.
"I leave in peace. I gave everything."
