b0c0a7a9bb02c8df: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.

This year is shaping up to be one of the hottest ever recorded. The world must begin to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions to address the climate crisis, which is already affecting communities around the globe. Wildfires, floods, and other climate-fueled disasters are killing thousands and costing billions of dollars. At the same time, political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress, particularly in the US.

Technology alone can’t solve climate change. But we believe innovations can help us make real changes and improve lives around the world as we try to address one of the most pressing challenges of our time.

In this project, we look for companies developing technologies that can help us face the climate crisis. Some are driving down the greenhouse-gas emissions fueling climate change; others are working to reduce the dangers that communities face from extreme heat, drought, or other shifts brought on by a warming planet. We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.

When we set out to build our list, we start by soliciting nominations from our team of reporters and editors. We ask experts for suggestions and reach out to academics, researchers, investors, and analysts. Once we have a pool of nominees, we then consider each one, digging through literature, reports, and patents to vet both the technology and the business.

We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall. We want the final slate of companies to represent a range of industries and include firms based around the globe that are at different stages of development. We also aim to strike a balance between highlighting companies previously included and introducing new names. Finally, we consider some of the most important trends and events of the year and look for nominees that reflect those developments.

The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech. Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US. China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate. This year’s list includes two Chinese companies: WeLion is building semi-solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, and Envision Energy is installing huge amounts of wind power and energy storage in China and around the world.
Several sectors stood out this year as being of particular importance. One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.

Energy storage is a key piece of that puzzle because it can smooth out variations in the electricity supply as grids incorporate more renewable power. We’ve included several energy storage companies on this year’s list. Energy Dome is building long-duration energy storage systems on the grid that rely on compressed carbon dioxide. Moment Energy is a Canadian company working to repurpose EV batteries for grid-scale storage. And Form Energy, which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.

A wide range of technologies is represented here: everything from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors. Some of the awardees might be familiar from our past coverage; others are just emerging and may be less well known.

We believe we’ve put together a list filled with businesses that are rising to the challenge of this moment. Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount. By helping us make progress on tackling the climate crisis in such difficult times, these companies point to a better way forward.
c4d30d0a93de2880: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones.
From the EVs that carry commuters home to the ships that transport goods across countries, more and more vehicles around us are powered by batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries are commonly used to power personal devices and vehicles today. But as the need for batteries surges, there’s a growing appetite for cells that can store more energy on a single charge.
Also, in lithium-based batteries the electrolyte, which facilitates ion transfer, uses a flammable liquid that can create a fire hazard.

Several companies, including WeLion New Energy, are working to make solid-state cells, which use a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. This could increase the energy density of batteries, as well as improve their safety. Fully solid-state cells are extremely difficult to manufacture, though. So WeLion currently focuses on developing and producing semi-solid-state cells, which have a part-liquid, part-solid electrolyte.

On that front, they have made steady progress. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack in partnership with Shanghai-based EV-maker Nio, best known for its battery-swapping technology. The pack had an energy density of 360 watt-hours per kilogram (wh/kg), significantly higher than the 200 wh/kg average for lithium-ion packs today. That translated to a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). However, only about 200 of the battery packs were manufactured due to their high production cost, but they are still being used by Nio, WeLion says.

WeLion has also built batteries to power cargo ships and ferries through a subsidiary. And the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density too. WeLion’s engineers made a semi-solid-state battery that achieved a remarkable energy density of 824 wh/kg during testing in 2025, more than three times that of a standard lithium-ion battery available today.
Key indicators
Industry: Energy storage
Founded: 2016
Headquarters: Beijing, China
Notable fact: WeLion’s cofounders include Chen Liquan, a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who led the development of the country’s first all-solid-state battery back in 1988.
Potential for impact

China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country, and its transportation sector accounts for around 10% of that total. Scaling up the production of safer, higher-capacity batteries could help switch more vehicles away from fossil fuels.

Batteries that power electric ships could be especially helpful—the carbon dioxide emissions from vessels that move goods along China’s lakes, canals, and rivers are projected to grow by around 25% in this decade alone, reaching 18.7 million metric tons by 2030.
Caveats

One big challenge WeLion faces is scaling up production of its semi-solid-state batteries and competing on cost in a crowded battery market. WeLion says that its semi-solid-state batteries are more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries made by larger Chinese battery companies such as CATL.

And while laboratory tests showing high energy density are impressive, it can be difficult to translate laboratory results to the real world. The company declined to give more details about the experimental results from its 2025 prototype, which it says is far from commercialization. Key details remain unclear, including how many times the cell can be charged and discharged and how capacity degrades over its lifetime.
Next steps

WeLion plans to bring a new semi-solid-state battery for drones to market with an energy density of 410 wh/kg by the end of this year. It also intends to introduce its first all-solid-state battery for cars in 2027, which is expected to have an energy density of 400 wh/kg.

Two inland cargo ships powered by WeLion’s batteries are expected to launch in October 2026 in Huzhou, a city in eastern China. The battery pack of each of these ships will be able to carry nearly 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough for them to sail for up to 250 kilometers (155 miles), the company says.

Today, WeLion has an annual manufacturing capacity of 11 gigawatt-hours (GWh) spread between four production bases in China. Two additional plants with a combined yearly capacity of 18 GWh are under construction.
ec8e04f2974057c9: Form Energy is building iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days. The company is ramping up supply at its factory and signing deals for commercial projects.

New solar and wind installations produce electricity more affordably than fossil fuels in most places, but their output varies based on season, time of day, and weather. To compensate, utilities are increasingly investing in battery storage systems, which can charge when power is abundant and discharge when the grid needs a boost.

Lithium-ion batteries are the fastest-growing storage technology. Although light and energy-dense, they require pricey metals and are costly to scale, and few of the large batteries of this type used in industry are designed to store energy for longer than four to six hours.

Form Energy wants to build cheaper long-duration energy storage technology. The company has developed a new type of battery, built with a far more abundant and cheaper metal, iron, that can store energy for 100 hours. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting.” During discharge, oxygen from the air converts the iron metal to rust, releasing electrons. When charging, current converts the rust back into iron metal.

Over the past two years, Form has gained commercial traction. It began producing batteries at its West Virginia factory for its first commercial deployment, a 150 megawatt-hour system for Minnesota electricity provider Great River Energy, which is set to come online in 2027. And Form has signed several other deals with power providers. The largest is a project with another Minnesota-based utility, Xcel Energy, where wind and solar power, backed by 30 gigawatt-hours of Form’s batteries, will be used to power a new Google data center. That project is expected to come online in phases between 2028 and 2031.
Key indicators
Industry: Energy storage
Founded: 2017
Headquarters: Somerville, Massachusetts, US
Notable fact: Once complete, Form’s proposed 30 gigawatt-hour energy storage system at a Google data center in Minnesota could be the world’s largest battery project by energy capacity.
Potential for impact

Wind and solar power play a major role in limiting growth in global carbon dioxide emissions. Still, many grid operators depend on fossil fuel plants, especially natural gas ones, to fill gaps caused by periods of low renewable supply or high demand. Form’s batteries are designed to cover multiday supply-demand imbalances, like those that crop up during heat waves, deep freezes, or periods with little sun or wind. The company declined to share the current cost of its battery systems, but says its goal is to reach $20 per kilowatt-hour, which would make them cost-competitive with the natural gas alternative.

The company’s technology could help reduce emissions from the AI data center boom. AI’s thirst for energy has already delayed closure of aging coal plants, led to the building of new natural gas plants, and caused price hikes for consumers. Cheap energy storage could help renewables meet more of this AI-driven growth in electricity demand.
FORM ENERGY
Caveats

The long-duration storage market is still nascent. Form’s iron-air technology faces a crowded field of approaches, including pumped hydropower, compressed gas, fuel cells, gravitational devices, and flow batteries that store energy in liquids. The economics of multiday batteries, which require large capital expenditures yet frequently sit idle, remain tricky.

While funding from data center developers could be a major boost, Form also has to prove it can deliver: Its existing production capacity, 2 gigawatt-hours of battery storage per year, is a fraction of the 80 gigawatt-hours it has promised through commercial agreements. Success will hinge on its ability to scale.

Another remaining question is the technology’s physical footprint. Form’s batteries, which are stacked together in enclosures the size of shipping containers, require an acre for every two to three megawatts. That means its Google installation would take up the equivalent of at least 75 football fields.
Next steps

In addition to finalizing its first commercial project, Form is outfitting its factory with new equipment that will help it scale manufacturing to meet its production backlog. It will do so with the help of new financing, announced in August, that brings its total money raised, in addition to West Virginia state and US federal grants, to more than $2 billion.
08ee819ff3370772: X-energy is developing small modular reactors to satisfy some of the planet’s most power-hungry users: industrial manufacturers that need high temperatures to produce billions of tons of concrete, plastics, fibers, and chemicals.

Solar panels and wind turbines are great at producing electricity but what heavy industry also needs is raw heat—and lots of it. The manufacture of concrete, glass, and steel, as well as the production of many chemicals, plastics, and fertilizers, are still highly reliant on fossil fuels to produce that heat.

Traditional nuclear reactors simply don’t get hot enough. The cooling systems they use require liquid water to work, and even applying pressure to raise the water’s boiling point leaves their maximum operating temperatures hundreds of degrees cooler than needed.

X-energy’s proposed Xe-100 reactor will use helium gas as a coolant instead, allowing it to operate at much lower pressures and higher temperatures. The helium will heat water and create super-heated steam, which industry can use either directly or to generate 80 megawatts (MW) of electricity via a turbine, or a combination of the two. That’s about one-tenth of the capacity of most reactors operating today.

In common with other small modular reactors (SMRs), the Xe-100 will use a modern uranium-based fuel called TRISO (short for tristructural-isotropic) that is extremely resistant to corrosion and melting. Compact TRISO “pebbles” will be added continuously to the top of the reactor, then flow slowly to the bottom, where they will either be recycled or removed as waste. The company says the reactor will be intrinsically safe in the event of a loss of power—if temperatures inside rise, the nuclear reaction naturally slows and stops.
Key indicators
Industry: Nuclear fission
Founded: 2009
Headquarters: Rockville, Maryland, US
Notable fact: The first helium-cooled reactor was proposed for the World War II Manhattan Project but was passed over in favor of a simpler and cheaper water-cooled design.
Potential for impact

Industrial heating currently accounts for 18 percent of annual global greenhouse-gas emissions, with about half of that coming from high-temperature processes that are difficult to electrify. Co-locating small nuclear reactors at large manufacturing facilities could shrink some of the biggest carbon footprints in the world.
The Xe-100 reactor could also be used by the fossil fuel industry, which today uses vast quantities of natural gas to generate the heat needed to recover oil from tar sands, and during oil refining.

The flexibility of the Xe-100 means that it can be used for traditional electricity generation. By scaling down in size and power from today’s gigawatt-scale fission plants, small reactors like the Xe-100 can serve more markets—even down to individual data centers. AI and data centers now represent the single largest component of new demand for electricity in the US, and their consumption is expected to double again by 2030. X-energy says that up to 12 of its reactors could be clustered together to provide 24/7 power on site, at a lower cost than a traditional nuclear power station and without the hassle of adding transmission infrastructure.
Caveats

The technology behind helium-cooled fission may be well understood, but the only commercial-scale power generation of this type today is in China, where two reactors have struggled to operate on a continuous basis. X-energy says that its vertically integrated fuel supply should ensure reliable operation, with reactors having a lifetime of 60 years.

The economic case for SMRs is also largely unproven. Nuclear costs and timelines have a habit of ballooning, and the US Energy Information Administration calculates that electricity from SMRs will cost more than six times that from solar farms. While the current environment in the US for regulation and government funding favors nuclear, that could change over X-energy’s long development time frame.

TRISO reactors appear excellent for safety and nonproliferation (the tough spheres would be difficult to turn into weapons) but are less impressive when it comes to waste. The Xe-100 might produce 10 times the volume of spent nuclear fuel per unit of energy as existing reactors, although its lower-level waste will need less sophisticated storage.
Next steps

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued X-energy’s subsidiary with a fuel fabrication license for TRISO-X pebbles, with its first factory due for completion in 2028. An Xe-100 to supply heat and power for a large chemical facility in Texas operated by Dow has also cleared its first regulatory hurdle, and could be operational by the early 2030s.

In tandem, X-energy is working toward a 320 MW cluster of four Xe-100 reactors in Richland, Washington, in collaboration with Amazon, and a larger 6 GW fleet in the UK’s northeast. Both projects target electricity generation in the 2030s.
159d30892a09abd6: There’s a growing need for long-duration storage to meet energy demand and balance out renewables on the grid. Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide gas in its massive grid batteries, which can deliver power for up to 24 hours.

As the world races to meet growing electricity demand, solar and onshore wind power have become the cheapest and quickest-to-deploy sources to install on the grid. But, despite their upsides, both are subject to variations in weather patterns, which means supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome is using stored carbon dioxide to help smooth out gaps between supply and demand.

The key component of an Energy Dome plant is a huge white dome that covers an area about the size of seven soccer fields and holds about 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide. When energy is available—say, from a connected solar farm—compressors squeeze the gas, turning it into a liquid that’s then stored in carbon-steel tanks. That process generates heat, which the system holds in a proprietary thermal storage material. Then, when the grid needs power, the carbon dioxide is released from the tanks and warmed with the stored heat, turning it back into a gas. That gaseous carbon dioxide then passes through a turbine to generate electricity and flows back into the dome, ready to begin the cycle again.

Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new—utilities have been using compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world.
Energy Dome turned on its first commercial plant in Sardinia, Italy, in 2025. The facility has a capacity of 200 megawatt-hours. That’s enough to power about 18,000 Italian homes for 10 hours.
Key indicators
Industry: Energy storage
Founded: 2020
Headquarters: Milan, Italy
Notable fact: Energy Dome has plans for 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of projects across five continents.
Potential for impact
Cheaper energy storage could help wind and solar meet more of the world’s electricity demand.

Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate new installations for short-duration applications of up to four hours. But the economics aren’t competitive for longer durations: A lithium-ion system that provides eight hours of storage at the same power output requires doubling the number of cells.

Energy Dome estimates that its technology is roughly 10% to 15% cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for an eight-hour system, and that the economics are even better for longer-duration systems of up to 24 hours. The company says its ability to scale bigger and faster than lithium-ion boils down to the fact that its design uses existing commercially available equipment like compressors and storage tanks. Its plants that are either operational or under contract have eight or 10 hours of capacity.
Caveats
Energy Dome only has one commercial project that’s operational. It’ll need to build many more to provide the 30 gigawatt-hours of storage it has planned.

The technology also isn’t quite as efficient as lithium-ion. Overall, Energy Dome’s process can return about 70% of the electricity it stores to the grid (a measure known as roundtrip efficiency). Lithium-ion batteries average roughly 90%. But some other long-duration storage techniques clock in lower; some iron-air batteries, for example, are around 50%.

Energy Dome’s plants may not all be benign from a planet-warming perspective. The company offers a version of its system that pairs its carbon dioxide battery with natural gas turbines. That version replaces internal heat storage with waste heat from the gas turbines to help evaporate carbon dioxide. That helps the plant run more efficiently but ultimately results in greenhouse-gas emissions from the natural gas turbines.
Next steps

Energy Dome has a pipeline of about 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants in the works around the world, and many of these projects could come online by the end of the decade. Because the company uses off-the-shelf components, the time from a signed contract to delivered capacity is only two years. In June 2026, for example, it signed a deal with Google to build a 200 MWh plant in Ireland, which is expected to come online in 2028.
e09aa4ef2a13bd42: Brimstone is making strides on two industrial problems, reducing the emissions from cement and providing a way to produce more critical minerals within the US. If the company can do both, with the same rocks in the same plant, it would unlock a cleaner and more efficient process for manufacturing building materials, aluminum, steel, and more.

Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US-based startup—part green cement company, part critical mineral producer—is well positioned to sustain its momentum no matter which party is in power.

During the more climate-focused Biden administration, the company’s primary pitch was its ability to produce cement while generating about 60% less greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when it’s heated. The conventional process for creating cement, the binding used to produce concrete, contributes about 8% of the world’s carbon dioxide pollution.

Under the protectionist and climate-denying Trump administration, however, the company is now stressing the secondary benefits of its process: the ability to extract other valuable materials from those same silicate rocks.

The company has said for years that its process could also generate materials that can be used to strengthen cement. But in early 2025, Brimstone highlighted that it would be able to also produce smelter-grade alumina, the raw material used in aluminum.
It then revealed it had another trick up its sleeve late last year: the ability to make steel, magnesium, titanium, and other critical minerals from the same rock in a single refinery.

The company’s CEO, Cody Finke, said those materials represent a $2.4 trillion global market. Brimstone’s approach promises to provide a domestic path for goods mostly produced today in China, the subject of Trump’s harshest trade policies and rhetoric.
Key indicators
Industry: Heavy industry
Founded: 2019
Headquarters: Oakland, California, US
Notable fact: In 2023, the company earned third-party industry certification for its process for manufacturing Portland cement, allowing its product to qualify for standard manufacturing projects.
Potential for impact

The company made a very big deal of its newfound ability to produce all these other goods, arguing its process would bolster national security and usher in the “next generation of industrial refining.” The basic environmental promise is that generating all these materials from the same rock and a single mining process would require dramatically less energy and produce far less waste than manufacturing them separately.
“I think that we have one of the generational companies that’s actually able to create an industrial revolution,” Finke says.
To which we would say: Well, we’ll see.
Caveats

Brimstone has yet to produce anything at a commercial scale, and it faces numerous financial and technical challenges. Some observers are dubious that the company will be able to economically extract sufficient quantities of so many materials from a single type of rock—or overcome the cost and labor issues that make mining and refining minerals a tough business in the US.

Brimstone also suffered a major stumble last year, when the Trump administration revoked a $189 million grant intended to subsidize its next plant, a planned commercial demonstration project in Reno, Nevada.

Finke says the company continues to have fruitful conversations with the administration about restoring those funds, in which Brimstone has emphasized its potential to boost domestic production of critical minerals. He has previously said the company will be able to proceed with the development of the plant, even without that grant or other subsidies.
Next steps

The company expects to begin operating the Reno facility, which will only produce cement, supplementary materials, and alumina, in 2028. That means Brimstone will still need to finance and build its first full-scale factory to deliver the steel, titanium, and other critical materials, likely pushing the timeline for doing so into the next decade.

Based on its progress so far, though, the company has already lined up several commercial deals. That includes agreements to supply cement to retail giant Amazon and alumina to Century Aluminum, one of the US’s largest producers of its namesake metal.
Even if Brimstone doesn’t bring about another industrial revolution, the company is equipped to slash emissions from cement, which is reason enough to pay close attention.

If Brimstone also manages to dramatically reduce the energy, pollution, and costs associated with extracting and refining rock to produce all—or any—of those other goods, that would represent a big corporate and climate win as well.
ad0eea6277cb0db1: As sea levels rise and flood risks worsen due to global warming, WaveSave’s easy-to-erect portable dam offers a quick-response tool. People can use the dam to protect themselves and their property, and it can also store freshwater for later use. Communities in Europe, Africa, and Southeast Asia have deployed it successfully. Now, the company is expanding into other water-related services to help vulnerable places become more resilient.

One in five people globally are at high risk of being exposed to serious floods. Many live in communities without proper protection and can’t afford to evacuate during a flood or relocate permanently. Climate change-driven extreme weather and sea-level rise is only exacerbating the problem.

WaveSave makes a portable rubber dam called SlamDam that customers can quickly install in the early hours of a flood. Anyone can unfurl it on the ground along a riverbank or shoreline and pump it full of water until it swells into place. And there it stands, up to 1.3 meters high, shielding nearby property or structures from damage as waters rise.

Developed in 2013 in the Netherlands, SlamDam was initially tested and is still used today by regional water authorities in that country. WaveSave has since expanded into Africa and Southeast Asia, and customers have now deployed SlamDam in at least a dozen countries.
Key indicators
Industry: Flood barriers
Year the company was founded: 2017
City and country of headquarters: Eindhoven, the Netherlands

Notable fact: WaveSave is demoing its SlamDam product on New York City’s Governors Island as one of seven winners in a competition for urban climate adaptations. The barrier is installed at a site where high tides and waves from passing ferries often wash ashore.
Potential for impact
Due to both climate change and population growth, nearly 2 billion people will be exposed to floods by 2100—an increase of 300 million from 2020, according to one estimate.

A SlamDam is designed to help protect farmland and personal property as well as critical facilities like hospitals or water treatment plants. It’s cheaper in the short term than more permanent modifications like building levees or rebuilding facilities on higher ground. And its temporary nature means it can be deployed as needed, and then stored away.
To fill the SlamDam, a local installer can use any portable water pump they may have on hand. With a lifespan of more than 40 years, the flood barriers can be used again and again.

This low-tech solution has another important benefit, at least when it comes to freshwater floods: In the weeks and months after a flood, residents can tap the water stored inside the mobile dam to irrigate crops. This is particularly helpful during the dry season or in drought-prone regions. At the rural Mpanda commune in Burundi in East Africa, where a SlamDam was deployed during the 2022 flood season, farmers with access to the water inside produced more crops that year and doubled their incomes, according to a UN report.
WAVESAVE
Caveats

Companies like AquaFence, MegaSecur, and NOAQ Flood Protection also make mobile flood barriers. WaveSave distinguishes itself in part by focusing on rapid emergency deployment in developing countries, and by emphasizing SlamDam’s ability to store water for later use.
But one research team that analyzed SlamDam’s use in Kenya found a series of challenges to getting communities there to adopt the technology. One was figuring out who should own and deploy the dam.

Another ongoing challenge is the up-front cost. SlamDam is already on par with or more affordable than many alternatives: It costs between €1,000 and €3,000 (about $1,140 and $3,400) per five-meter section, and comes in a range of heights. Protecting a single entrance to a home or facility might require only 10 meters, while surrounding a facility (such as a hospital) or shielding a farm or neighborhood might take 200 to 300 meters. But the price is still too high for many communities or farmers. WaveSave’s managing director Omar Saleh says the company is looking into offering SlamDam as a service and deploying it on demand to make protection more affordable.
Next steps

Right now, an external partner manufactures all SlamDams in the Netherlands; they are then shipped to customers based elsewhere. But WaveSave aims to open a local production facility for SlamDams in Southeast Asia in early 2027, followed by a similar facility in East Africa, which could help lower costs. The company recently won contracts for four new projects totaling about $5.3 million in Burundi, Djibouti, and Guinea, with a “substantial pipeline” developing in Southeast Asia and Latin America, according to Saleh.
The company is currently self-financed and only has seven employees. Saleh says he plans to grow organically by investing profits back into the firm.

Part of that growth will involve offering new services such as advising communities on how to install and operate simple, off-the-shelf rainwater harvesting and irrigation systems, as part of a more comprehensive approach to managing water in climate-stressed regions.
685812927dfa92b2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 6 — Malaysia needs tax reform to address a structural decline in its tax revenue-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, which has fallen to 12.7 per cent from 15 per cent 15 years ago, according to the World Bank lead economist Apurva Sanghi.

He said the federal government debt has risen to over 65 per cent of GDP although the fiscal deficit has been contained, however, this would not be enough to bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down to the target of 60 per cent by 2028.
“Federal government debt rose despite the contained deficit and now stands at 65.2 per cent.

“The cost of servicing debt is also increasing, with 17 sen of every ringgit in revenue raised spent on debt servicing,” he told the media during a briefing on October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update here today.

Yesterday, the Auditor General’s Report 2/2026 reported that federal government debt stood at RM1.32 trillion in 2025 compared with RM1.24 trillion in 2024, while the statutory debt stood at RM1.295 trillion, comprising Malaysian Government Securities, Malaysian Government Investment Issues and Malaysian Islamic Treasury Bills.
Apurva said that while increasing tax rates would be difficult, there were ways to raise tax revenue without doing so.

Responding to a question on taxation and Budget 2027, which will be tabled this Friday, he said simplifying the corporate tax system for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) by consolidating the tax structure would benefit businesses.

029f0b40edc8d12d: From Salahuddin Hamzah
I refer to a column by Tajuddin Rasdi, published on Oct 5.

I am furious with this theory. The writer’s argument, which suggests that Malays accept corruption, has little merit and is substantially unfair because it omits many important historical events. Let’s look back at the timeline.

Between 2014 and 2018, corruption was perceived to be at its peak due to the 1MDB scandal. What happened afterwards? Umno-Barisan Nasional was overwhelmingly voted out by the rakyat after ruling the country for 60 years.
In 2022, BN only won 30 seats. Isn’t it evident that the perceived corruption was rejected by the Malays?

After each defeat, Umno accepted the result wholeheartedly and openly welcomed investigations into allegations of corruption. Many leaders paid a heavy price, either through jail time, fines, or damage to their reputations. The leadership repeatedly called for the party's revival. Yet the writer has refused to factor this into his argument.
The writer also claims that the majority of Malays pay little to no tax. This is an old song.

In reality, a large segment of Malaysia’s M40 population are Malays, and they pay taxes. The M40 are also largely working-class salaried employees, meaning the taxes they owe are automatically deducted from their income, leaving little room for tax avoidance.
In comparison, many of the much wealthier T20 taxpayers are business owners, where tax costs can potentially be transferred to consumers.
Let’s not even go into the largely non-Malay-dominated black market, which operates tax-free and involves billions of ringgit.

Regarding DAP as the bogeyman, the writer seems unable to accept the very nature of democracy – voters can choose freely. DAP being dominated by one race simply does not appeal to the majority of Malays. Marketing wise, DAP is a failure. But the writer refuses to acknowledge this.
The Malays' lack of preference for DAP is instead portrayed as an acceptance of corruption. What kind of argument is this?
I firmly believe that the conscience of the Malays is entirely clear – Malays do not accept corruption. Any argument suggesting otherwise is simply racist and simplistic.
When former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted, Umno accepted the judgment with an open heart and "keinsafan" (remorse).
No one took to the streets claiming that the conviction was illegitimate. Umno only sought a royal pardon, which is a form of clemency provided for under the Federal Constitution.

The leniency shown by some Malays towards Najib is in no way an acceptance of corruption. It is substantially fuelled by the frustration that after Umno’s defeat, things do not seem to have gotten better.
Najib deserves his partial pardon considering his significant contributions to the country, despite the shortcomings.
I reject the writer’s theory.
Salahuddin Hamzah is an Umno Youth member and an FMT reader.

a4beae4315c8e89c: From Syerleena Abdul Rashid
I keep thinking about the plans Irene Sofiya Khairool Faisal had made with her friends.

After their examinations, they wanted to spend some time together, celebrate their birthdays, dress up and go out for coffee. They were ordinary teenage plans. The kind young people make without imagining that anything could stop them. Irene was 16. She wanted to become a doctor, like her late mother. On Oct 3, she was found badly injured inside her school hall in Yong Peng. She died before help arrived.

A student has been remanded and the police are investigating the case as murder. The motive has not been established, so we should not speculate or try the case on social media. Still, one fact should trouble every parent in this country – Irene went to school and never came home.

Just days later, Parliament was told that 5,681 bullying cases had been reported in schools between January and August this year. The cases included physical, verbal, non-verbal and cyberbullying. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself acknowledged that the real number could be higher because some cases might have gone unreported.
That number bothers me. But what bothers me even more are the children who may not be included in it.

How many kept quiet because they were frightened? How many tried to tell an adult but were dismissed? How many parents were told that it was only a misunderstanding between students? How many schools worry more about their reputation than the child asking for help?
We have been here before.

Last year, Malaysians were shaken by the death of 13-year-old Zara Qairina Mahathir, who was found unconscious near her boarding-school dormitory in Sabah. An inquest into the circumstances of her death has been ongoing, alongside separate proceedings involving allegations of bullying. We must allow those legal processes to establish the truth. Zara deserves facts, not rumours.

We also remember Zulfarhan Osman Zulkarnain, who was tortured by fellow university students and died from his injuries in 2017. Seven years later, the Court of Appeal convicted six former students of his murder.

These cases are different. We should not pretend that every school incident has the same cause or circumstances. But each of them forces us to ask whether the adults, rules and institutions surrounding our children are doing enough to keep them safe.
The honest answer is that we are still falling short.

I appreciate the prime minister’s willingness to admit that current measures are not enough. The government has increased counselling support, trained wardens, strengthened disciplinary procedures and mental-health screening, and allowed the police greater access to schools. More CCTV cameras are also planned.

These steps matter. But installing cameras cannot be the whole answer. A camera may record what happened. It cannot comfort a frightened child, notice a sudden change in behaviour or ask why a student has stopped eating, talking or attending class.
That requires people who are trained, alert and prepared to act.

Every serious complaint should have a clear deadline for action. The child must first be placed somewhere safe. Evidence must be preserved. Parents must be informed. Counselling and medical support must be available immediately. If a possible crime is involved, the police and child-protection authorities must be notified.

Children also need a way to report abuse outside the immediate school hierarchy. It is extremely difficult for a young person to complain when the alleged bully is a senior student, or when the person who ignored the earlier complaint is someone in authority.

We should also publish anonymised data regularly. How many complaints were received? How many were investigated? How long did schools take to respond? How many were referred to the police? What support was provided to the victims?

This is not about humiliating teachers or treating every school as unsafe. Most teachers work extremely hard and care deeply about their students. It is about ensuring that those who do their jobs properly are supported, while those who conceal complaints or fail to protect children are held accountable.

Parents have responsibilities as well. We must pay attention when our children become unusually quiet, angry or afraid to attend school. We must listen before blaming them or telling them to toughen up. But parents cannot be inside classrooms, corridors and hostels throughout the day. Once a child enters the school gate, the institution assumes a duty of care. That responsibility cannot disappear when something goes wrong.
Bullying is not character-building. Fear is not discipline. Keeping quiet does not protect a school’s good name.

A school earns its reputation when children feel safe enough to learn, speak and ask for help. That is the standard we should insist upon, because no family should have to send a child to school in the morning and spend the evening wondering why that child never came home.
Syerleena Abdul Rashid is the Bukit Bendera MP.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

64c8aa7272839624: Sweden is the home of bork, and what better way to mark it than with a huge example of digital signage that shows a GRUB message instead of an ad? GNU GRUB (the GRUB is short for Grand Unified Bootloader), according to GNU, "is responsible for loading and transferring control to the operating system kernel software." In this case, the user has some options. UEFI firmware is one. Some options for DMS are another. DMS might mean Dank Material Shell, unless you know better. It's an attractive enough desktop, but it seems like overkill for something that slings ads for the few seconds Stockholm commuters raise their gaze from their devices. Some enticing possibilities are on offer. Hitting "e" will edit the commands while "c" will drop the user into the command line. That's assuming, of course, that the user is carrying a keyboard to attach to the stricken screen, something we're sure every Register reader has in their backpack, but not something civilians would necessarily keep on their person. GRUB has featured in this column before, appearing on a UK bus after a filesystem became a bit poorly (motion sickness can clearly affect computers as well as commuters), but this is a wall-sized example of the breed. Judging by the passengers on the escalators opposite, it appears that nobody is rushing to the aid of the stricken signage. That's probably for the best – leave it for a few seconds (by the looks of things), and it'll have another go at booting. Still, it's always good to see GRUB putting in an appearance in a section often dominated by Windows and Android whoopsies. The era of the Linux desktop might not be upon us just yet, but judging by this Stockholm signage, bork is alive and kicking in the open-source world. ®

4319adb01862650c: OpenAI is now offering API customers the option to watermark the output of certain models in order to comply with the letter of Europe's AI Act. And within a few weeks, the biz plans to apply a form of digital watermarking – like it or not – to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union. But unlike rival Anthropic, it isn't applying its watermarking technique to content generated outside of Europe, though API customers can choose to have the marks applied to content made anywhere. Moreover, OpenAI is using technology that misses a fair number of instances of AI-generated text and can easily be tricked. The EU AI Act requires generative AI service providers to make model output identifiable in a way that's readable by machines. Anthropic was the first major AI company to announce its approach to AI Act compliance, which involves the application of Google's SynthID-Text algorithm. It's doing so globally. Microsoft and Meta have been working on similar technology for image-based AI because the EU is not the only market in which people have raised concerns about content provenance and the potential to use AI-generated content to produce misinformation. OpenAI already applies other content provenance signals to AI-generated images, audio, and video. In keeping with the letter of the AI Act, OpenAI is now offering a text watermarking approach called textGrain [PDF] that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark." Large language models predict word tokens one at a time from a probability distribution of potential words. By picking a different word to emit periodically – ideally a synonym – the resulting text deviates from the statistical pattern produced by an unbiased model. A watermark detector, which OpenAI is making available only to approved researchers and organizations, should flag that vocabulary divergence. That's the theory, but in practice results vary. The target error rate is one percent, but in short passages of 200 words, the detector may only flag 80 percent of the watermarks, compared to 95 percent in a 400-word passage. The results are also worse in texts that are functional, like passages about math or code, as substitutions are more likely to introduce errors. The textGrain paper does not address the likelihood that a statistically altered word choice might alter the meaning of a given passage. That's a possibility if the algorithm were to alter some salient fact or figure. Anthropic's approach, which also replaces certain output words though using a different algorithm, brings similar risks. In any event, OpenAI's watermark is easily defeated by word substitution. In tests on 400-token passages, swapping out 10 percent of the words with synonyms reduced watermark detection from 92 percent to 66 percent. And when replacing 25 percent of words, the watermark signal could only be detected in 17 percent of cases. Now witness the firepower of this barely adequate but compliant AI detector… ®
054817028c3de88e: When yellow dwarf stars like our sun die, they swell to an enormous size and destroy their inner planets by either crushing them with massive gravity or evaporating them with astounding heat. While these suns later settle down to become a white dwarf, the process is nearly always game over for planets in an inner solar system. Or maybe not, according to a paper published on Monday titled “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” As explained by NASA’s Hubble Mission team, the paper’s authors pored over Hubble Space Telescope observations of white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 from 1999. According to the paper, data from those scans “revealed the presence of carbon, aluminum, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere, as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified.” The authors of this paper used new techniques to identify the mystery matter, and concluded that there’s plenty of the element niobium present in what looks like a gas giant orbiting HS 0209+0832. In NASA’s post, co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin, pointed out that “Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion.” “Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star's innards into space.” Finding niobium is also notable because, as the paper explains, “the canonical rock-forming elements [are] silicon and iron.” The paper explains that its authors compared the material observed at HS 0209+0832 with all known examples of rocky material around white dwarfs, and to all meteorites in our Solar System, but could find “no compositional matches.” That finding suggests that the niobium-rich gas giant at HS 0209+0832 represents both a secondary planet – which are rare – and a body composed of material we’ve not previously seen becoming a planet. It also shows that planets can form close to a star after the hellish red giant phase. Oh, and let’s not forget that HS 0209+0832 is also an exoplanet, a class of body humanity first spotted in only 1992. The paper suggests the niobium gas giant is about the size of Jupiter, but that the white dwarf is blasting away its atmosphere and perhaps creating “a comet-like tail of material that would form a disk around the white dwarf star and fall back on to its surface, leading to Hubble detecting the niobium when studying the star” Co-author Jamie Williams, from the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, told NASA he thinks the niobium world will stick around. “If the second-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years,” Williams said. ®

7959c958d7cb3069: From Kua Kia Soong

Malaysia is not merely buying ships late. We are buying fewer ships for more money – and may receive the first one before it is actually capable of fighting. That is the extraordinary reality exposed by the latest auditor-general’s report.

The littoral combat ship (LCS) project is now 7.55% behind schedule, with the first vessel, LCS 1, itself 13.88% behind schedule. Its physical handover, already postponed from August to December 2026, may now be pushed to April 2027.

But that is not the worst of it. The government may eventually receive LCS 1 without the full combat capability that makes it a warship in the first place. So, what exactly are we celebrating when the ship is "handed over"? Six became five – and RM9.13 billion became RM11.23 billion.

Let us start with the basic arithmetic. The original LCS contract was for six ships at RM9.13 billion. After restructuring, Malaysia is getting five ships at RM11.23 billion. That is fewer ships for more money. And by June 2026, RM8.56 billion – 76.22% of the revised contract value – had already been paid.
An accountability crisis

For an ordinary household, paying more and receiving less would be called a disastrous bargain. For a government procurement programme involving billions of ringgit of public money, it should be called something more serious: an accountability crisis. The government cannot keep telling taxpayers that the project is "progressing" merely because more money has been spent and more steel has been assembled.

The question is not how much has been spent. The question is: what has Malaysia actually got for the money? A warship without weapons? The most surreal possibility is that Malaysia could take delivery of LCS 1 while essential weapons and support systems are still unresolved.

Five critical complementary contracts remain unfinalised. The most serious problem concerns the surface-to-surface missile system. Because of problems involving the export approval for the original missile system, Malaysia faces the prospect of having to procure an alternative. The audit estimates that this could involve three years of negotiations, followed by six years for production and delivery. In other words, the navy could receive its first LCS while waiting years for one of its principal weapons.

This is where bureaucratic language becomes almost comical. A ship can be physically delivered. A contract can be declared substantially completed. A minister can stand beside it for the obligatory photograph. But if the ship cannot perform its intended combat mission, Malaysians are entitled to ask: is this really the warship we paid for – or merely the most expensive floating work-in-progress in Malaysian history?
A major procurement timeline shift

This is where the LCS saga becomes more than another story about delays. For years, Malaysians have been told that the project is being rescued, restructured and put back on track. Each time the deadline moves, we are given another explanation. Each time the cost rises, there is another justification. Each time another problem emerges, we are told that the project must continue because too much money has already been spent.

Now we appear to be approaching a new definition of success. Success no longer means delivering a fully operational combat vessel. It means handing over the vessel. The distinction is crucial. A physical handover is an administrative event. Combat readiness is a military capability. They are not the same thing. And according to the auditor-general's findings, full operational capability could stretch all the way to 2035. That is not a delay. That is a major procurement timeline shift!
Who is accountable?

The LCS saga has now gone on for so long that there is a danger Malaysians will simply become numb to each new announcement. In 2011, the Najib Razak administration approved the project and Ahmad Zahid Hamidi was the defence minister.

A letter of award for the RM9.13 billion project was issued to Boustead Naval Shipyard (BNS) on Dec 16, 2011. The official formal contract for the construction of the initial six ships was signed a few years later, on July 17, 2014. The restructuring of the LCS project down to five ships was finalised under the Anwar Ibrahim administration in early 2023. The finance ministry officially stepped in and took over BNS, and the company was subsequently restructured and renamed Lunas.

Someone must ultimately answer for the decisions that produced this extraordinary situation. Who approved the original procurement arrangements? Who was responsible for ensuring that the ships, weapons systems, logistics and training requirements were properly integrated? Why were essential complementary contracts left unresolved? Why did the original six-ship programme become a five-ship programme at a substantially higher cost? Why should taxpayers accept a vessel before it possesses the full capability for which it was ordered? And most importantly: who will be held responsible if Malaysia finally receives five ships costing RM11.23 billion, only to discover that the navy still does not have the fully operational fleet it was promised?

Parliament cannot simply rubber-stamp the next cheque. This is precisely why the LCS project cannot be treated as a routine procurement matter buried somewhere in the defence ministry's accounts. It is a test of parliamentary oversight.

The government should table a complete accounting of the project's original and revised costs, all variations and supplementary contracts, payments made, penalties imposed or waived, outstanding liabilities, and the precise timetable for achieving full operational capability.

And Parliament should insist on one deceptively simple distinction: when will Malaysia receive the ships – and when will Malaysia receive the combat capability it paid for? Those are two different dates. Malaysians should not be asked to confuse them.

The auditor-general has given us the numbers. Now Parliament must demand the accountability. And after all these years, the Malaysian taxpayer deserves to know when the story finally ends – and when the navy finally gets the ships it was promised.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP and former Suaram director.

75a585434004ff74: Linux KVM, the hypervisor favoured by hyperscale clouds, apparently has a full VM escape bug. That nasty news came from security researcher Paulos Yibelo, who on X shared a screenshot of a bug bounty award he won for discovering what he described as “Full VM escape zeroday (guest>host root in industry standard hypervisors)!” The bug bounty Yibelo participated in is run by Vercel, a company that provides MicroVMs as sandboxes for AI agents to work inside. The company’s Sandbox uses Firecracker MicroVMs, a technology created by AWS, which relies on Linux KVM – the kernel level hypervisor in Linux. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch named KVM as the hypervisor identified by Yibelo. “We’ve confirmed a KVM 0day through our Vercel Sandbox bounty program. Affecting the industry’s gold standard solution for Linux virtualization,” he wrote. And that’s all the info that has made it into the public view at this time. The Register can find no chat on relevant mailing lists. We have asked Rauch and Yibelo for additional details. Hopefully, we don’t hear from either of them for days or weeks, for two reasons. One is that guest-host escapes are the nightmare virtualization scenario because they mean whoever runs a guest VM could take over an entire server, and perhaps gain the ability to control other guests. The other is that KVM is astoundingly prevalent: AWS and Google both use it to power their public clouds. Enterprise virtualization players Nutanix, HPE, and Proxmox also rely on KVM. And of course KVM is also in Firecracker, which is open source and could therefore be running in all sorts of places. Whatever Yibelo discovered therefore very much needs a responsible disclosure process, because if hints about the flaw emerge it could allow attackers to do a lot of damage. Once a fix is found, the next question is whether implementing it will require disruption or downtime. It’s possible to hot-patch KVM, and to migrate live VMs from vulnerable hosts to machines running a patched version of Linux. Hopefully those techniques will work. This might be the second nasty bug discovered in KVM this year, after the so-called Januscape flaw. Beyond the potential risks this bug created, observers have suggested the potential seriousness of the flaw means Yibelo’s reward should exceed the $50,000 available under Vercel’s bug bounty program. ®
6500841de5f4e302: Baru-baru ini terjadi perbualan panjang di medsos dalam kalangan penggiat filem, peminat dan penonton apabila filem Terbang arahan Chiu Keng Guan, pengarah yang pernah menghasilkan filem OlaBola dan The Journey itu gagal mencapai kutipan yang memberangsangkan. Selepas seminggu ditayangkan, Terbang dilaporkan hanya mengutip sekitar RM1.2 juta, angka yang agak kecil bagi sebuah produksi menelan belanja sekitar RM10 juta. Filem diinspirasikan daripada perjalanan legenda rali Malaysia, Karamjit Singh dan pasukan PERT itu mula ditayangkan pada 17 Sept 2026. Barisan pelakonnya bukan calang-calang. Ada Irfan Zaini, Jack Tan, Nam Ron, Zizan Razak dan Shweta Sekhon. Kegagalan ini menimbulkan tanda tanya apakah filem biopik tempatan tak berapa diminati oleh penonton kita? Di sinilah gaduh-gaduh berlaku terutama di Threads. Saya meneliti hujah demi hujah.

Saya tidak berkesempatan menonton filem Terbang. Ramai penonton yang telah menontonnya memuji dan mengiktiraf ia sebagai sebuah filem yang baik. Soalnya, mengapa sebuah filem yang dipuji baik tidak mendapat sambutan seperti yang diharapkan? Perkara begini bukan pertama kali berlaku. Macam selalu, setiap kali sebuah filem yang dikatakan bagus itu gagal, akan timbul kenyataan yang sama baik daripada penggiat filem, begitu jugalah khalayak – salah penonton! Penonton kita dikatakan tak cukup bijak menilai filem, lebih menggemari filem ringan dan kosong seperti filem…ah! Tak usahlah kita beri contoh. Tapi kita boleh nampak. Memang ada filem tempatan yang meletup berpuluh juta dan kita tahu filem jenis apakah itu.

Penonton dipersoalkan mengapa mereka tidak mahu tonton filem seperti Terbang sedangkan filem 'yang sana itu' boleh pula laku? Tak pasal-pasal penonton kena jawab di medsos. Macamlah mereka sudah buat salah besar, padahal mereka cuma tidak membeli tiket untuk menonton. Kritikan itu ada asasnya tapi kalau asyik penonton sahaja yang dipersalahkan, menyampah pula dibuatnya. Sebuah filem yang bagus dengan sebuah filem yang orang mahu tonton itu tidak sama. Sebuah filem boleh dibikin dengan bagus tetapi semua itu belum tentu akan membuat seseorang rasa terdorong untuk pergi menontonnya. Bagus itu pun subjektif sifatnya.

Ada banyak faktor memungkinkan orang tak masuk panggung. Mungkin genrenya, barisan pelakonnya, atau strategi promosinya gagal memukau. Boleh jadi juga waktu tayangannya tidak kena. Ia bertembung dengan pilihan-pilihan lain yang lebih disukai. Tapi, satu hal misteri yang saya rasa wujud.

Saya pernah bertanya kepada S Amin Shahab, seorang seniman terkenal kenapa belum pergi menonton filem 'anu' itu? Ketika itu ada sebuah filem biopik politik tanah air juga. Jawab beliau, 'tak ada seru nak pergi tengok.' Itulah maksud saya tadi. Produk nampak macam dah sedap tapi entah kenapa, tak membuat kita terpanggil. Bab ‘seru’ inilah bagi saya misterinya.
Saya teringat juga petikan kata-kata pengarah U-Wei Shaari: “Kita boleh buat filem yang cerdik kalau ada audiens yang cerdik," (‘Hanyut Akhirnya Sangkut’ oleh Israr Khalid, Astro Awani, 13 Okt 2016).

Saya faham maksud pengarah yang sangat saya kagumi itu. Sesetengah karya memang untuk penonton yang mahu berfikir, mempunyai pengetahuan sedia ada yang tinggi dan sanggup menyingkap mesej tersirat di sebalik kisah yang diperlihatkan di layar. Tetapi izinkan saya untuk 'ganggu' sedikit ungkapan itu. Apakah masalah ‘filem cerdik melingkup’ ini akan selesai jika penonton sudah jadi cerdik? Katakanlah masih berlaku filem gagal, siapa pula yang hendak kita salahkan?

Kecerdikan seseorang tidak juga menjadikan dia menyukai filem yang dilabelkan sebagai cerdik. Seorang pensyarah (cerdik, kan?) misalnya, selepas memberi kuliah di universiti, dia balik ke rumah dan mungkin memilih untuk menonton cerita hantu di Netflix. ‘Mat sastera’ yang membaca novel Fyodor Dostoevsky mungkin mempunyai selera yang baik dalam memilih filem tetapi ada ketikanya dia cuma mahu menghibur hati dengan menonton komedi mengarut seperti The Naked Gun. Saya pun setelah penat sepanjang hari bertekak soal idealisme dan falsafah, memilih filem komedi ‘deadpan’ lakonan Jason Bateman. Lega sikit rasanya.

Ia tentang selera. Ada banyak benda yang bagus tetapi ia tidak semestinya dapat menepati selera semua orang. Selera bagi saya, bukan ujian IQ. Bukan apa, kita kena berlaku adil juga kepada penonton. Filem-filem ‘cerdik’ pernah sahaja laku dan mendapat kutipan tinggi pada zamannya seperti ‘Fenomena’, ‘Selubung’ atau ‘Perempuan, Isteri dan…’

Apabila ramai penonton memenuhi pawagam untuk filem yang kita anggap bagus, kita gembira mengatakan masyarakat sudah pandai menghargai karya bermutu tetapi apabila mereka memenuhi pawagam untuk filem yang kita nampak lekeh, kita memperlekehkan pula selera mereka.

Tak adil jugalah kalau asyik penonton saja yang kena sekolah. Contoh mudahnya begini, suatu hari ketika kita sedang duduk makan dan berbual dengan kawan-kawan di sebuah restoran, datang seorang peniaga membawa keropok dari meja ke meja. Dia berhenti di meja kita dan menawarkan keropoknya. Kalau kita suka, kita beli. Kalau tidak mahu, kita geleng kepala dan dia bergerak ke meja lain. Kita tidak perlu membeli semata-mata kerana takut dia berkecil hati. Kalau kita hendak beli pun sebab kita memang suka keropok itu dan harganya berbaloi. Mungkin juga kita tidak suka sangat tetapi kerana kita ada duit lebih dan berkemampuan, kita beli. Orang yang bersifat budiman memang ada. Ia tidak salah.

Tetapi barang diingat, itu simpati, bukan selera. Katakanlah kita enggan membeli, tak patutlah peniaga tadi marah kita kerana tak mahu menyokong usahawan tempatan seperti dia, kan? Keropok dia jual, duit kita punya. Kalau setuju, ia akan bertukar tangan dengan rela.

Begitulah juga dengan filem. Kita beli tiket kerana tertarik dengan ceritanya dan segala elemen yang dipertaruhkan di dalamnya. Kita juga boleh membeli dengan niat mahu menyokong industri filem tempatan. Malah kalau mahu membeli kerana simpati pun tidak salah. Tetapi akhirnya ia adalah tentang pilihan. Sebab itu saya rasa tidak patut jugalah kita memaksa penonton memikul tanggungjawab moral untuk menyokong filem tempatan. Seolah-olah begini: penerbit filem sudah berhabis duit. Pengarah dan pelakon sudah bekerja keras. Kru bersengkang mata dari mula sampai tamat produksi. Lalu, menjadi tanggungjawab masyarakat kitalah untuk menyokong kerja keras para karyawan ini. Patutkah?

Ya, tetapi kita semua adalah ‘karyawan’ (bermaksud pekerja dalam Bahasa Indonesia) yang bekerja keras juga. Peniaga keropok tadi pun bekerja keras. Pelukis, kerani, pemandu Grab semuanya bekerja keras. Mereka pun pergi tonton wayang jika ada kemampuan. Tetapi kena fahamlah, menonton wayang hari ini bukan sekadar beli tiket. Kalau pergi berkeluarga, kena kira kos makan, minum, petrol dan parkir. Bukan kecil punya modal. Jadi, penonton berhak berkira-kira produk hiburan mana yang mahu dibelinya. Kalau kena tepat dengan selera mereka, pasti mereka tak teragak-agak berbelanja.

Jangan pula salah faham. Ini tidak bermaksud pembikin filem mesti menurut sahaja selera pasaran. Kalau filem hantu laku, letihlah kita kalau semua nak buat filem hantu. Kalau filem aksi laku, tak payahlah semua nak buat babak kejar-mengejar di atas bumbung deretan kedai atau semuanya nak buat adegan kereta meletup. Menyampah pula kita menengoknya nanti. Karya yang mencabar selera semasa perlu dibuat. Filem eksperimental perlu ada. Filem yang perlahan, aneh, berat atau berbeza juga berhak wujud. Kalau semua pembikin mengejar apa yang sudah terbukti laku, seni tidak bergerak. Tetapi sudah tentulah keberanian membuat sesuatu yang berbeza datang bersama risiko. Ini memang satu perjudian dan adakalanya hanya keajaiban jadi penentuan. Mudah kata, ia bersangkut juga dengan rezeki dan nasib.

Kalau kita mahu membuat filem yang tidak mengikut selera semasa, kita juga perlu bersedia menerima kemungkinan bahawa selera semasa memang jarang menyebelahi filem seperti itu. Dari situlah kita perlu mengkaji. Hasil kaji selidik tersebut pasti lebih berguna daripada kita terus mempersoalkan IQ penonton. Kalau sebuah restoran lengang, pemiliknya akan melihat kembali menu, harga, lokasi, servis dan promosinya. Jarang kita melihat tauke restoran berdiri di pintu memarahi orang yang lalu-lalang kerana tidak mahu masuk makan. Itu pandir namanya.

Saya seorang penulis yang telah menghasilkan beberapa buah buku. Saya tahu betapa pedihnya hati apabila melihat orang ramai membeli buku penulis lain dan bukan buku saya. Tapi saya tahu kenapa, apa kekurangan saya. Yang membeli buku saya, saya sedapkan hati dengan kata-kata, 'mereka inilah jauhari yang mengenal manikam.' Yang tak beli, saya sejukkan hati dengan sebab tak menepati citarasa dan selera mereka. Ada juga kawan-kawan yang membeli kerana menyokong. Ini kerana mereka berkemampuan. Dalam industri apa pun, kita perlukan orang begini. Berkemampuan dan menyokong. Ada yang berkemampuan tetapi tidak juga membeli buku saya. Takkan saya nak marah?

Filem memang medium seni yang paling pantas sampai ke mata masyarakat. Tetapi sebaik sahaja tiket mula dijual, bermakna ia telah memasuki dunia pilihan pengguna. Di sinilah untung nasibnya bakal diuji. Filem memang hak pembikin untuk dibuat sebagaimana yang mereka mahu. Tetapi tiket tetap hak penonton untuk membelinya atau tidak. Sama seperti peniaga keropok tadi. Kita boleh beritahu orang keropok kita sedap. Kita boleh suruh orang yang sudah makan memberikan testimoni. Kita boleh jelaskan betapa susahnya hendak membuat keropok itu. Tetapi kalau orang di meja itu masih tidak mahu membeli, bukan bermakna dia tak suka keropok. Bukan juga sebab IQ dia rendah. Mungkin dia sedang menimbang-nimbang isi poketnya sama ada berbaloikah beli keropok atau lebih 'afdhol' makan nasi.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.

You need not be a Rafizi Ramli enthusiast to accept that after Anwar Ibrahim vacates the role of Pakatan Harapan (PH) supremo or is obliged to do so from GE16 failure, there is no one else to take up the position.

This point is best made by former PKR youth religious leader Wan Ji Wan Hussin who in recent remarks opined that there is a void in PKR (and by extension, PH) as to who should re-take the reins of leading the movement for reform in the country.
Wan Ji held that prior to his leaving PKR last May, Rafizi provided the analytical framework and political messaging for PKR and, by implication, for PH.
He observed that Rafizi’s energy and ability to simplify complex matters equipped him for the role of standard bearer of the reformasi movement.
As the Bersama leader it will take two more general elections before he is accepted as the supremo of the reformasi movement.
He will get to that position as head of Bersama in a shorter span if he and his cohort presently avoid taking away votes which would otherwise go to PH parties in the upcoming Melaka polls.
Bersama performed poorly in their inaugural electoral foray in Johor and then wisely decided to skip the Negri Sembilan polls to re-gather their strength for a Melaka outing.
Wong Chen, the former PKR MP for Subang who has since joined Bersama, declared that the party wants to garner 12% of the vote in Melaka in comparison to the six percent it took in Johor.
This would be a negligible increase if realised and would almost certainly come from votes that would otherwise go to DAP, PKR and Amanah, the tripartite combine that composes PH.

A wiser trajectory in the prelude to GE16 which must be held by February 2028, would be for Bersama, which is actually a splinter party of PKR, to concentrate on the 10 seats (of the overall 31 seats) that PKR won in GE15.
These seats are quite easily identifiable as seats that the Rafizi cohort occupies in PKR.
Some of the occupants have already come out in support of Bersama while others presumably would wait for the dissolution of Parliament before declaring so.
This strategy is wise because Bersama would avoid incurring the resentment of PKR, DAP and Amanah in the current phase of choosing to politic without actual electoral participation.
Bersama should just wait until GE16 is announced and then go for the seats PKR won in GE15 that are held by Rafizi’s tacit supporters who are just biding their time in PKR.

It’s not that PKR does not know who these tacit supporters are. Just look at what the party leadership has recently done by allowing former PKR MPs Edmund Santhara (Segamat), Kamaruddin Jaafar (Bandar Tun Razak), and Steven Choong (Tebrau) to return to the fold.
The trio were elected in GE14 but abandoned PKR for Muhyiddin Yassin’s Bersatu in early 2020 to enable Muhyiddin to become prime minister.
That foray ended in a dead-end.
Bersama would be better off by holding to what it can reasonably hold instead of looking for what may be prospectively — but not actually — theirs.
Patience and realism are key for Bersama.

2cc21a3abc84d45d: From Moaz Nair

In multiracial Malaysia, authentic patriotism requires an objective, rigorous engagement with historical truths. To achieve this, secondary school curricula must prioritise critical inquiry over passive, uncritical acceptance.

For generations, history classrooms have functioned as secular chapels where students are expected to passively consume, memorise and venerate state-sanctioned narratives. While educators frequently assert that the primary goal of history education is to instil patriotism, a fundamental question remains unaddressed: what paradigm of patriotism is being cultivated?

A superficial patriotism built upon sanitised, heavily curated myths leaves a citizenry intellectually fragile. Conversely, a robust allegiance to the nation demands cognitive rigor – specifically, the academic courage to evaluate the past objectively through a critical lens.
Loss of historical nuance

Requiring students to accept textbook narratives without question does a disservice to both pedagogical standards and democratic citizenship. History is not a static ledger of undisputed facts; rather, it is a dynamic, ongoing dialogue between the past and the present, woven from the varied perspectives of both dominant and marginalised actors.

When school curricula reduce complex epochs to oversimplified, nationalistic narratives, they degrade a dynamic discipline into mere rote memorisation of dates and nomenclature. The deficiencies of this approach become evident when analysing the systemic omissions and oversimplifications within history textbooks.

A pertinent case study is the traditional pedagogical coverage of the 1875 assassination of J.W.W. Birch, the first British Resident of Perak. Students are conventionally taught that Birch was assassinated due to his interference with local customs, or adat Melayu.
Birch and debt slavery
However, curricula routinely omit the crucial, uncomfortable specificities of this interference: Birch’s aggressive campaign to abolish debt slavery.

By shielding students from this complex reality – wherein a colonial figure maintained a morally justifiable stance against human bondage while operating within a flawed imperialist framework – the curriculum privileges narrative convenience over historical accuracy.

This obfuscation of structural realities is indicative of a broader trend of presenting historical events in a unilateral vacuum. Prominent local historians note that in recounting the pivotal Pangkor Treaty of 1874, textbook narratives frequently replicate outdated colonial tropes, attributing British intervention strictly to internal royal disputes and secret society clashes.
Consequently, they obscure the crucial roles played by early capitalists who actively bankrolled and manipulated these regional factions to secure lucrative mining monopolies.
Structural amnesia

Beyond structural simplifications, recent curricular omissions risk fracturing national identity. Recent iterations of the secondary school syllabus have drawn sharp criticism from academics for downplaying the monumental economic and foundational contributions of Malaysia's plural society.

The exhaustive efforts of early Chinese and Indian communities in transforming the nation’s tin mining and rubber industries – alongside the significant loss of life during the construction of Malaya's foundational railway and road infrastructure – have been increasingly minimised compared to older editions.

Erasing the labour and sacrifice of minorities and indigenous groups from the master narrative implicitly signals to students that only select demographics contributed to the nation's state-building process.

Critical analysis of historical narratives within the pedagogical text exposes frequent contradictions, omissions and discrepancies. When scholars and students interrogate these reductive frameworks, they inevitably find that it presents a highly sanitised or biased rendering of the past.

These instructional flaws underscore the urgent need for a pedagogical shift from passive consumption to critical analysis. Teaching history through a critical framework involves training students to interrogate authoritative texts, cross-examine competing primary and secondary sources, and identify the ideological motivations underpinning historical documents.

Addressing “historical amnesia” requires unearthing the untold narratives of marginalised or uncomfortable perspectives, whether dealing with the harsh realities of colonialism, internal socio-political injustices or structural inequalities.
Civic engagement

Opponents of a critical historical framework often express concern that questioning established narratives will erode national pride. However, empirical observations suggest the opposite: institutional propaganda and state-sanctioned distortions breed civic cynicism.

In contrast, an evidence-based approach to history fosters deep civic engagement. When students are trusted to evaluate historical evidence, recognise systemic bias, and navigate the nuances of human conflict, they develop the vital analytical skills necessary to decipher propaganda and participate meaningfully in a pluralistic society.

If educators intend for students to contribute to an equitable future, curricula must move away from demanding the memorisation of a single, immutable story. Classrooms must equip students to participate in historical dialogue and independent critique.

True patriotism does not demand cognitive blindness regarding a nation's historical blemishes or cultural diversity; rather, it requires a comprehensive understanding of these elements to construct a more honest and inclusive society.

Educational institutions must confront the realities of the past. A transparent evaluation of historical trajectories is foundational to building an equitable future and inspiring authentic patriotism. Therefore, secondary history education must never devolve into an exercise in political indoctrination.

In an increasingly interconnected global information ecosystem, suppressing uncomfortable historical truths is an unsustainable strategy; inquisitive students and parents will inevitably uncover alternative narratives omitted from the formal classroom.

Ultimately, confronting an authentic past with an open mind does not divide a population; instead, it empowers a society to build a fairer future and fosters a deeper, more resilient love for the country.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
